articles.title: Transcript: Mayor Mamdani Hosts Gaggle
articles.content: Governor Kathy Hochul: It's great to be back in Puerto Rico for the 40th gathering of Somos, joined by our chair of Somos, Karines Reyes, also Frankie Miranda, the head of the incredible Hispanic Federation. And a great partner of mine in governing is our mayor, Zohran Mamdani. And I want to thank all the representatives from El Puente, which means the bridges, right? We're building bridges between New York and Puerto Rico every way we can. I want to thank them for their participation in this roundtable. We talked about the needs of this community, particularly in light of a historic drought, but also the ongoing challenges with the resiliency of the grid and the delivery of water, etc. So, we found some ideas. I've already told my team we were going to be delivering even more, so stay tuned for some post-conference announcements. Question: I have a question about — for Mayor Mamdani and Governor Hochul, while you're down here — Mayor Mamdani, I know you're going to a meeting for the Esencia Project. Question: Do you support Council Member Alexa Avilés’ resolution supporting efforts to block the project? And will you visit Cabo Rojo — and for the both of you — sorry not to ignore you, Governor Hochul — will you visit Cabo Rojo, which is the town where the project is located? Mayor Mamdani: I'm looking forward to the meeting this afternoon with Puerto Ricans, including [those] from Cabo Rojo, to speak about the impact of this project. And to me, that is one of the most critical parts of being here in San Juan, is also having this be an opportunity to listen to Puerto Ricans about the ways in which New York City and New York State can stand in solidarity with them. I'm not as familiar with the specifics of the Council member's resolution, but I will look at that and get back to you. Question: And who will, I mean, will it be people who are opposed to the project as well because there was some concern about the infrastructure issues and it was still passed through by the Puerto Rican government? Mayor Mamdani: I think a lot of the people that we'll be meeting with have been on the front lines of pushing back against this project, and they're going to be illuminating why. Question: And you, Governor Hochul, as well? Governor Hochul: No, I'm going to stay in touch with the people on the ground here and ask them [about] their concerns. I'm not familiar with the legislation. Question: Could you tell me what hopes do you have that things for Puerto Rico will change or improve given the results of the midterms? Mayor Mamdani: Well, I think we've seen a few days ago a new chapter in our country's history, and there's a potential in that, that we can finally start to deliver for working-class people across this country, and what we heard today was the fact that so often what's described as a natural crisis here in Puerto Rico is in fact a political crisis, one that is the result of political choices. And we're excited that we are starting to take different political choices across our country, and we hope to see different political results. Governor Hochul: Particularly, the influence of the Puerto Rican community is very strong in New York State and New York City. And to have leadership in Congress that knows those challenges from firsthand and representing them, I think, is a real advantage. This is not a community that has to be understood. It is well understood by our leaders in Congress that we'll be sending there. Secondly, it's a whole new day of responsibility of the federal government to Puerto Rico. And what we've seen over the last two years is really an abandonment of that commitment. And we hope to have all those wounds heal, making sure that we continue bringing resources for resiliency, energy projects, building up the grid, as well as healthcare being restored, nutrition programs. And so, I would say it's a whole new day for Puerto Rico with this election. Question: Governor Hochul, coming off your decisive win on Tuesday, will you now renew your pledge to not raise taxes in New York State? And then separately for you, Mr. Mayor, you know, you have a lot of officials down here this year, a lot of commissioners, a lot of deputy mayors; this is your first term in office in Somos. Who authorized the fire commissioner coming here with four staff, and what is her agenda here? Mayor Mamdani: So, the fire commissioner, Lillian Bonsignore, is here as part of long-standing administrative practice to have a number of representatives from our administration here at this conference. And her primary responsibilities, they range from meeting with legislators, meeting with government partners, as well as meeting with local fire officials to exchange best practices. And I think you've heard from the governor earlier that whenever Puerto Rico has been in a crisis, we've sought to be there. And we also heard from a number Puerto Rican leaders today that the best way to prevent the next crisis is to prepare in advance of it, and we view the bond between our city and Puerto Rico as an unbreakable one, one that also requires us to share as much as we can across government officials. Question: Just following up with Governor Hochul. Governor Hochul: My takeaway from the election is that the voters of New York State have overwhelmingly supported our policy agenda. They want me to keep fighting to deliver affordability for New Yorkers. They want me to keep building more housing. They want me to focus on energy resiliency and focusing on the threat of climate change. And the other major one is childcare. And I will work hard to manage within our existing resources, but if we need more, we'll find a path as I've done before. When there's a particular need, a very specific need, like helping the city just less than a year ago with the Pied-à-terre tax, a dedicated revenue source for a specific purpose to help the city. Or the time we had to stop the MTA from going literally off a fiscal cliff when I first became governor, had to increase the revenues coming in from the payroll mobility tax. So, I want to make sure that we have a path forward that is sustainable to fully fund childcare, because this is how New York will be defined for generations to come: did we have the ambition, the boldness, but also the resources to make sure that that is guaranteed for many years to come? Question: Governor, given the question that Craig just asked, I was wondering if you see a need for the legislature to come back this year to finish any unfinished business? We just started talking about taxation— Question: You have leveraged your relationship with the president in a number of immigrant success stories in terms of getting the Ghanaian mother to the United States and releasing an Algerian student at Columbia University when she was in detention. Because we're at Somos, which is really centering Latino leadership, I just wondered if you could talk a little bit about what immigration looks like for that community; given that you have a relationship with the president, but now you have [a] more progressive Congress. So, could you just outline what you see as some of your commitment to the Latino community? Mayor Mamdani: Absolutely. It is a commitment to ensure that Latino New Yorkers can continue not only to live in New York City, but to flourish in New York City. And what you have heard today has also been the stories we've heard in New York City. We heard about stories of people who don't want to leave their homes out of fear of ICE here in Puerto Rico; those are the same stories we hear in New York City. And what we talk about — the governor and I care deeply about public safety. And one of the reasons I'm so opposed to ICE's immigration enforcement actions is because they do nothing to contribute towards that safety. In fact, they threaten that safety. We're talking about an agency that opened fire on a moving vehicle in broad daylight, right after school was let out, opening fire on a man and his five-year-old child. And what that does, it instills fear in New Yorkers about their ability to leave their homes, live in their neighborhoods, live the lives that they sought to live. And we hear it from New Yorkers; we hear it from small business owners; we hear from, you know, our brother Frankie Miranda; we hear that from anyone who interacts with Latino New Yorkers, because it is a fear that has become in some senses almost permanent since we've seen this kind of federal policy. And as the governor said, it feels like a Michael Bublé song: “It's a new day, it's a new dawn.” It is a real opportunity for us. It's a real opportunity for us in our country to finally see the values of humanity reflected also in federal policy. Governor Hochul: There is a tremendous opportunity for Congress to finally do what this country has been asking for in red states and blue states, which is a common-sense policy related to immigration; increasing the legal entrance to bail-to-commit; dealing with border issues, yes, but also making sure that we deal with asylum seekers in a very different way; and to stop the overreach of ICE in small communities in upstate New York, the streets of New York or here in San Juan. And that's something that I believe will be a benefit to this country rejecting Republican leadership in Washington. They have had enough. In a nonpartisan way, they've had enough for the overreach of ICE. So, I'm familiar with immigration reform. I worked on a bill when I was an attorney for Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan before most of you were born. But it was a path that the country could work together on — a Democratic House, Republican president at the time — and they got it together and had meaningful reform. I think the possibility is there. If Donald Trump wants to try to create a different legacy than one he's going to leave with in two years, one of it could be doing something that has been breaking that stranglehold on not being able to move forward on meaningful immigration reform, because I think our country is hurting when we don't open the doors to people who want to come here to get an education, to be able build their families, start new businesses for us. And that's something I'm expecting from this Congress as well. Question: What was I asking you — whether you see a need for the legislature to come back this year to finish any particular unfinished business and on the question that Craig raised, are you saying now then that if you see a need, potential income tax increases are on the table? Governor Hochul: I've always operated that way; that is not a newsflash. That’s how I’ve — if you look at my record, I've reduced taxes, the largest middle-class tax rate cut in seven years, but when I've had to find the resources to further policy goals like keeping the MTA alive, I did that. When it came to helping the city out in a severe financial crisis that the mayor inherited, I stepped up with a creative way to do that. I'm telling you that I want to find a creative path to make sure we have the resources necessary to be able to have a long-term commitment to childcare. I said we got through this year; I'm committed to next year. But now that we have the time to put together a thoughtful approach to how we make sure this is here for decades to come, I'm going to continue doing that. articles.title: Powerful Haitian gang reaches out to state disarmament group as gunfights persist
articles.description: Powerful Haitian gang reaches out to state disarmament group as gunfights persist AP News El Salvador’s president thinks he can eliminate Haiti’s gangs The Economist ‘Potentially ugly’: taking war on gangs to Haiti poses risks for El Salvador’s leader The Guardian Powerful Haitian gang leader tells AP he wrote UN seeking dialogue as clashes intensify AP News Why is El Salvador fighting Haiti’s gangs? GZERO Media
articles.content: SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — One of Haiti’s most powerful gangs said Friday that it reached out to a government agency responsible for dismantling armed gangs in a push for “peace, stability and national reconciliation.” The 400 Mawozo gang sent a three-page statement to The Associated Press stressing that “dialogue is not a capitulation,” but rather an “act of patriotic responsibility to preserve human lives.” The United Nations and human rights groups have accused 400 Mawozo of raping, killing and kidnapping people, which it has denied. On Nov. 1, gang leader Wilson Joseph told the AP that he wrote to the U.N. secretary-general and requested that the organization send a delegation to Haiti for dialogue and mediation amid fears that the presence of Salvadoran troops could further escalate violence. The gang, which refers to itself as a rebel group, said that it plans to participate in a peaceful demonstration later this month “in order to lay the groundwork for a national dialogue and peace negotiation process.” “Haiti’s future cannot be built solely on confrontations and military operations,” it said. Haiti’s National Commission for Disarmament, Demobilization, and Reintegration told the AP that an individual contacted them on behalf of the armed group, but that the commission works alongside the prime minister’s office. “For any dialogue with armed groups, we must follow the roadmap proposed by the government,” the commission said. The letter was shared as Haitian police and foreign forces continue to battle gangs, with Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé announcing on X late Friday that a gang leader was killed, without identifying him. Haiti’s National Police said the leader of the Boston gang known as Mathias was one of those killed in a joint operation with other law enforcement forces. Mathias was a well-known gang leader that operated out of Cité Soleil, a gang-controlled slum in Port-au-Prince. “The gangs won’t be getting any sleep!” the prime minister wrote on X. Police said in a statement that several gang members were injured and killed in the operation as it urged Haitians to turn over their “illegal weapons” so that “they can change their lives.” The AP reached out to a spokesperson for 400 Mawozo and asked if the gang is willing to lay down its weapons. The person, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they don’t want to be publicly identified to talk about these issues, responded that the gang is willing to engage in peace negotiations and that disarmament is a process. When asked what 400 Mawozo seeks in exchange, the person said peace and the end of what they called “international interference.” The gang’s announcement comes just weeks after El Salvador deployed more than 2,000 troops to Haiti following the disappearance of four Salvadoran aviation technicians who came under attack on Oct. 18 while deep in gang territory. The United Nations has said that most of the Salvadoran personnel in Haiti are operating outside the framework of the U.N.-backed gang suppression force that is working with Haiti’s police and military as well as Vectus Global, the private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince. The gang said it believes it would be “beneficial” if all “relevant military forces” suspend operations targeting certain areas pending the “effective opening of a dialogue on peace and stability.” “This period should provide an opportunity for de-escalation, the protection of civilian populations, and the search for a lasting political solution,” it wrote. In its letter, 400 Mawozo said it was worried about social media posts “targeting” the home of Joseph, best known as Lanmò Sanjou, especially comments attributed to El Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele. On Friday, Bukele responded to a social media post in which he was tagged and allegedly showing Joseph’s home. “Where is that house? Give us the exact address, and we’ll destroy it,” Bukele wrote on X. In its letter, the gang described Joseph’s home as “a symbol of peace within the framework of its de-escalation process” and called on “all parties to respect international obligations relating to the protection of civilians and civilian property.” The gang referenced certain articles within the Geneva Conventions as well as the Charter of the United Nations. El Salvador’s government declined to comment when reached by the AP on Friday night.

articles.content: Food is a focal point on Thanksgiving. Turkey is the traditional centerpiece, but side dishes garner their share of the glory, too. Stuffing, mashed potatoes and vegetable casseroles have a way of finding their ways onto the Thanksgiving menu. But hosts looking to offer something a little more unique this year can look to this delicious recipe for stuffed zucchini from Lines+Angles. Stuffed zucchini for Thanksgiving. Image by Metro Creative Connection Stuffed zucchini Makes six servings Six medium zucchini, washed and ends trimmed 3 cups butter cracker crumbs, crumbled 1⁄2 cup grated Parmesan cheese, plus extra to sprinkle One small onion, peeled and minced 3 tablespoons minced fresh parsley, plus extra for garnish Freshly ground black pepper, to taste 1 teaspoon salt Two eggs, beaten 2 tablespoons butter 15 ounces canned diced tomatoes, drained well 1. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. 2. Cut the zucchini in half lengthwise and scoop the pulp out with a spoon. Place the zucchini shells in a large baking pan. 3. In a large bowl, combine the zucchini pulp, cracker crumbs, cheese, onion, parsley, salt, pepper and beaten eggs. Fill the zucchini shells with the mixture, then dot each with butter. Spoon the tomatoes over the filling, sprinkle with additional Parmesan cheese and bake for 30 to 35 minutes. Garnish with chopped parsley and serve.

articles.title: That Candy Store satisfies the sweet tooth of nostalgia
articles.description: Name that iconic type of candy that sends you back to childhood: Charleston Chews, 5th Avenue bars or the Candy House Candy Buttons. They might not be stocked in the […]
articles.content: Name that iconic type of candy that sends you back to childhood: Charleston Chews, 5th Avenue bars or the Candy House Candy Buttons. They might not be stocked in the candy aisle of Meijer or Walmart, but Lansing residents can still find their childhood favorites, right in the heart of Old Town. Step inside That Candy Store, located at 1232 Turner St., and the nostalgia of youth comes flooding back. Shelves are stocked with long-lost classics, like candy cigarettes and Mallo Cups. Owner Jim Coyer wants to help customers reconnect with childhood moments. “People can come in and find a few minutes of happiness,” he said. “Happy treats and sweet memories kind of go hand in hand.” The idea came from the neighborhood candy store where he grew up shopping. “I remember the feeling of walking in the door,” he said, “you know, my eyes got all big.” Coyer specifically added sugar candy sticks, inspired by the field trips he took as a kid to Frakenmuth, which he described as some of his fondest childhood memories. That Candy StorePhoto by Lieza Klemm/City Pulse The store’s stock is not only a collection of Coyer’s personal favorites. Customers’ suggestions help shape the inventory, with visitors often requesting candies they remember from childhood. Some products are discontinued, but others stir Coyer to research and track down new additions. “Every time you come in here, there’s something new,” he said. Unlike other stores in the area that satisfy a sweet tooth, Coyer designed the store’s inventory to inspire nostalgia. “I hear a lot of stories every day from people who come in and say, ‘Oh, I haven’t seen this since I was a kid’,” he said. That Candy StorePhoto by Lieza Klemm/City Pulse The store also features Michigan-made products, including Mackinac fudge and Towne Club Soda. Coyer hopes to incorporate more treats from Michigan companies, like Hannah Chocolates in St. Johns and Cherry Republic in Traverse City. Although they are a priority, Coyer acknowledged the state’s candy manufacturing industry limits how much of the store’s inventory can be sourced locally. Coyer sells an impressive assortment of 21 saltwater taffy flavors. He said the inventory is always changing, but the pickle and rocketpop flavors are bestsellers. “You can find saltwater taffy at most candy places, just not like this.” In the store’s second room are more products, sure to unearth buried memories. Coyer stocks the timeless Rock ‘Em Sock ‘Em Robots and Barrel of Monkeys tabletop games, along with scratch-and-sniff stickers. “I’m trying to find things that can bring back those memories and those feelings of happiness,” Coyer said. Ultimately, Coyer hopes That Candy Store becomes a local staple where customers can escape their daily routines and reconnect with fond memories. “It is your neighborhood candy store where you can come in and immerse yourself in sweet memories for a little while.”

articles.title: Flu season is starting early, so experts say get the vaccine ASAP if you haven't already
articles.description: Michigan's flu season got an early start this year, and health experts say nearly everyone should get a flu shot as soon as possible so their immune systems have time to gear up for possible exposure.
articles.content: Doctor, healthcare expert and medical worker with plaster on arm of sick child after covid vaccine, help with medical emergency and consulting with patient at hospital. Girl with bandage after injury.(Nina Lawrenson/peopleimages.com - stock.adobe.com / 527959530)The influenza season is arriving early this year. Experts say flu cases began showing up on the West Coast in September.Ryan Malosh is director of the Immunization Division at the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services. He said emergency department visits for flu-related illness are now starting to tick up in Michigan, and that means people who haven't gotten their flu shots yet should do it now. He said it takes about two weeks after getting the flu vaccine for the body to develop antibodies and provide protection against influenza."When cases are really spiking, the last thing you want to do is be caught without its protection, so it is definitely a good time to get it," Malosh said.The flu vaccine doesn't always keep people from getting the flu. But it can significantly reduce the severity and duration of symptoms, along with the risk of hospitalization and death. Children are among the groups that are most vulnerable to flu. In the 2025-26 influenza season, more than 1,600 children in Michigan were hospitalized due to flu, and 13 children died, according to state health department data.Other groups that are particularly vulnerable to flu include pregnant women, elderly people, and people with immune system disorders. But even healthy adults can become very ill from flu.Dr. Adam Lauring, the chief of infectious diseases at Michigan Medicine, said matching the vaccine to the variants that are likely to be in circulation each year is not easy work. This year, the vaccine does include the H1N1 variant that is most in circulation, but early reports indicate it may have a mutation that makes the vaccine less effective, especially for younger people."We don't know yet," Lauring said. "We won't know until later in the season. But I think the message still is, go out and get your vaccine."

Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Kathy Hochul travel to Puerto Rico for annual conference, discuss support
articles.content: PUERTO RICO (WABC) -- Gov. Kathy Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani traveled to Puerto Rico this week, where they joined other elected officials for the annual Somos Conference and discussed support for the U.S. territory following Democrats' midterm election victories. The two leaders appeared together Tuesday and spoke optimistically about the political landscape following what they described as a Democratic "blue wave." Mamdani said the election results could create new opportunities for working-class Americans. "There's a potential in that, that we can finally start to deliver for working class people across this country," said Mamdani. Hochul said she hopes the federal government will renew its commitment to Puerto Rico. "It's a whole new day of responsibility of the federal government to Puerto Rico. And what we've seen over the last two years is really an abandonment of that commitment and we hope to have all those wounds heal," said Hochul. The governor's remarks came after Democrats swept the midterm elections, a result she said would help provide accountability and strengthen support for Puerto Rico. Hochul and Mamdani were among a group of elected officials attending the annual conference on the island, which has faced challenges including chronic power outages and water shortages. The governor said Democratic control of Congress could help secure additional resources for Puerto Rico and address immigration enforcement concerns. "And to stop the overreach of ICE in small communities in upstate New York, the streets of New York or San Juan," Hochul added. The visit also highlighted the longstanding ties between Puerto Rico and New York City. The report noted that Latino voter support for Donald Trump increased nationally in the previous presidential election but polling showed a decline in that support during his second term. While discussing governing priorities, Mamdani said he intends to continue working with Hochul despite any policy differences. "I've always been clear about where I stand. I continue to to to hold those positions. I'm also looking forward to continuing a productive working relationship with our governor to deliver for working people," Mamdani said. As both leaders advance their policy agendas, they said cooperation between city and state government will remain a priority.

articles.content: OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion. Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects. OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

articles.title: TWTS: When a wave becomes a tsunami
articles.description: The midterm election coverage was inundated with talk of not just waves but potential tsunamis, none of which, of course, involved an inundation of water.
articles.content: The midterm election coverage included plenty of talk about waves and even tsunamis. But while the political kind may have dominated the headlines, "tsunami" refers to something far more destructive than a political shift.Before tsunami showed up in English, speakers used "tidal wave." The phrase dates back to at least 1715, when it referred to waves connected to the tides. By the mid-1800s, it was also being used to describe massive ocean waves caused by earthquakes and volcanic eruptions — what we now call tsunamis.Tsunami came into English in the late 1800s. Early newspaper accounts often included an explanation for readers unfamiliar with the term, describing a tsunami as a “sea wave” or “earthquake wave.” Its use became much more common in the early 2000s, particularly following the devastating Indian Ocean tsunami in 2004.By the 1970s, "tsunami" had also started appearing in figurative expressions. Today, news coverage uses it to describe everything from political shifts to surges of anger, racism, data, and support.The New York Times this week published an article about the response in Japan to the use of "tsunami" to describe this week's “blue wave.” As you might expect, not everyone is comfortable using a term associated with catastrophic destruction to describe political movements, including a so-called “blue tsunami.”There's also the question of pronunciation. The Japanese pronunciation includes a “t” at the beginning, but English speakers often drop it. Both pronunciations appear in many dictionaries, reflecting the way borrowed words often adapt to the language that adopts them.To hear more about "tsunami," including its pronunciation, listen to the audio above.

Doctors pull knife from man's eye that went through his brain—and he's fine now
articles.description: It's the exact path, not the apparent severity that matters most, doctors say.
articles.content: A man in his 20s showed up to a UK hospital with the hilt of a knife sticking out of his face. The 15 mm-wide blade hidden within went completely through his right eye and through his brain, with the tip of the blade hitting the top of his skull. Despite the ghastly injury, the man was alive and conscious when he arrived. He could still talk and move all four limbs. His doctors described him as being in a state of agitation. On the Glasgow Coma Scale, he scored a 12 (E3 V4 M5), indicating a "moderate" brain injury, just one point above "mild." He could open his left eye when told, but otherwise kept it closed (E3 score); he could talk and answer questions, but was confused (V4); and he intentionally moved away when pressure was applied to his body (M5). In a report published Friday in BMJ Case Report, his doctors said they were concerned that in his confused, agitated state he may try to pull the knife out on his own. So, they swiftly sedated and intubated him. They put him on prophylactic treatments for bacterial infections, including tetanus. Then they used images to see what was going on in his head.Read full article Comments

articles.description: OpenAI has reportedly raised an additional $11 billion as part of a funding round that hasn't closed yet but is expected to in the coming weeks.
articles.content: OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion. Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg. In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target. TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds. The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago. OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point. The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market, with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future. articles.content: Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz—a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack such undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed US and Israeli strikes. The movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat have been tracked near major undersea cables by the maritime intelligence firm Windward in October, according to the Financial Times. Six active cables currently cross through the contested Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa and Asia, with two more cables having segments under construction in the region. Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, depend entirely upon such subsea telecommunications connections running through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint to link with the outside world. But other countries also depend heavily on the region's undersea cable network—one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Displaced residents of Leland House in Detroit to get $15K each
articles.description: The settlement, which could exceed $500,000 in total, was obtained by the Detroit Tenants Union on behalf of the 37 residents, who were forced to evacuate the 21-story downtown high-rise last December.
articles.content: Detroit Free Press is a partner and shares a reporter with BridgeDetroit. Stories shared are not under a paywall. Detroit Free Press Former residents of the Leland House apartments in downtown Detroit are to each get $15,000 as part of a bankruptcy court settlement that a judge approved the week of Nov. 2. The settlement, which could exceed $500,000 in total, was obtained by the Detroit Tenants Union on behalf of the 37 residents, who were forced to evacuate the 21-story downtown high-rise last December after an electrical outage caused by broken equipment in the building. Steven Rimmer, chair and executive director of tenants union, described the settlement, which was approved Thursday, Nov. 5, as a significant victory for the displaced renters and an outcome that doesn’t happen often in Detroit for those in similar situations. The money is to be dispensed in the coming weeks. “Residents lost their homes, were separated from their belongings and were left to navigate a crisis that turned their lives upside down,” Rimmer said in a statement. “They could have been forced to face this alone. Instead, they organized, stood together and fought.” The Leland House, 400 Bagley St., was known for its cheap rents and all of its tenants were on month-to-month leases. The equipment failure and forced evacuation happened about a month after Leland House declared bankruptcy. U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Maria approved the settlement, with money for the $15,000 payments to come out of the proceeds from the building’s recent $3 million sale. Court documents say that money was available for the tenants because city officials were willing to forgo “a large portion” of Detroit’s own claims in the bankruptcy court case. Because some of the displaced tenants had nowhere to go, the city for months paid the bill for them to stay at a Red Roof Inn in Southfield. The tenants also had to wait nearly five months for permission to go back inside the shuttered apartment building to retrieve their belongings. Conrad Mallett Jr., the city’s Corporation Counsel, told the Free Press on Friday, Nov. 6, that the city ultimately incurred over $750,000 in costs for temporary housing for the Leland House residents, and anticipates collecting less than $150,000 from the bankruptcy case. “To be sure that the tenants could live their lives in a hopefully new and better circumstance … we absolutely chose to forgo dollars that would have reimbursed us, in an effort to make sure that each family could get started anew,” he said. The bankruptcy judge approved the sale of the empty building this spring for $3 million to a limited liability company called Mudhish Development, linked to businessman Raad Gobah. Gobah previously declined to discuss his group’s future plans and did not respond Nov. 6 to messages seeking comment. Mallett, the city’s attorney, said he is also unaware of what the building’s new ownership may be planning to do. “Saying that you’re going to redo the Leland House is a herculean task,” Mallett said. “So we’re interested in what the new owners plan, and to the degree that they approach us with a solid plan, we would certainly be interested in trying to be supportive.” The building opened in 1927 as the Detroit-Leland Hotel and was renamed Leland House in 1964, when the property became a mix of hotel rooms and apartments. The late Detroit landlord and developer Michael Higgins bought the building in 1980 and went on to open a popular nightclub inside, known as Leland City Club, which was known early on as a hard-core punk venue and that evolved over time with more techno, goth and industrial music. Harper Woods man charged in Warren bank robbery
articles.content: A 56-year-old Harper Woods man was arrested and arraigned Friday on the allegation he robbed a Warren bank three days earlier. Roylee Darryl Buck, Jr. was charged with bank robbery, a life offense, in 37th District Court in Warren hours after he was captured in Harper Woods in possession of evidence related to the robbery, according to Warren police and Macomb County prosecutors. Warren Police Commissioner Eric Hawkins credited investigators in the department for their work in identifying Buck as the alleged culprit and locating him. “Thanks to the swift, precise work of our investigators and the seamless coordination with our federal and local partners, a dangerous suspect is off the streets tonight,” Hawkins said in a press release. “This rapid arrest shows the relentless commitment of the Warren Police Department to keep our city safe.” Buck allegedly robbed the Huntington Bank at 10 Mile and Ryan roads on Election Day when he presented a note to a cashier demanding cash while implying he possessed a weapon, police said. The employee complied, and the suspect fled the scene with an undisclosed amount of money. Warren detectives interviewed witnesses and gathered other evidence including local surveillance footage. The investigators identified Buck as the suspect using forensic and other evidence. The FBI and Warren Police Special Operations Unit and Special Response Team apprehended Buck in Harper Woods. Buck was charged as a four-time habitual offender, which could impact his sentencing. His criminal history dates back to 1986, with prior felony convictions including breaking and entering, carrying a concealed weapon, fleeing police, and assault, according to police. At the time of this arrest, he was on parole for a federal bank robbery conviction Judge Michael Chupa set Buck’s bond at $1 million cash-or-surety. He is scheduled to appear Nov. 17 for a probable-cause conference in front of Chupa, prosecutors said.

articles.title: What could the blue wave mean for economic policy in Michigan?
articles.description: University of Michigan economist Betsey Stevenson explains what Democrats' election victories could mean for inflation, AI, data centers, and Michigan's economy.
articles.content: People watch returns come in before Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed arrives at a Michigan Democratic Party election night event, early Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, in Detroit. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson / AP Photo)Economist Betsey Stevenson said Democrats have gained voters' trust on economic issues — an area where Republicans have traditionally held an advantage.Stevenson said newly elected Democrats should focus on affordability, tariffs, and health care costs rather than getting distracted by efforts to hold the Trump administration accountable.AI investment has helped drive overall economic growth, but Stevenson questioned whether that growth is creating enough jobs or raising wages for everyday Americans.Attracting innovative companies and long-term employment opportunities could be more valuable than the temporary construction jobs associated with new data centers, Stevenson said.Democrats won major victories in Michigan and across the country in Tuesday's midterm election. In Michigan, voters elected Jocelyn Benson as governor and Abdul El-Sayed to the U.S. Senate, while Democrats secured majorities in both chambers of the state Legislature.But with affordability and the economy among voters' top concerns, what will Democrats need to do to deliver on their campaign promises?Betsey Stevenson, a professor of public policy and economics at the University of Michigan's Ford School, joined Stateside to discuss what the election results reveal about voters' economic priorities and what they could mean for Michigan's future.Stevenson said one of the biggest developments is a shift in which political party Americans trust to manage the economy.For decades, she said, Republicans maintained an advantage on economic issues, even when their policies weren't necessarily producing better outcomes. But recent surveys have shown a growing belief that Democrats can do a better job."That was a really tough nut for Democrats to crack," Stevenson said.Now, she argued, Democrats need to demonstrate that they can address the economic concerns that helped bring them into office.Stevenson said newly elected lawmakers should prioritize measures aimed at reducing costs for consumers, including rolling back tariffs, and restoring Affordable Care Act subsidies. She also pointed to the economic impact of the war in Iran and its effect on oil prices.While voters may also want greater accountability from the Trump administration, Stevenson cautioned that Democrats risk losing sight of the issues that helped them win.Another major economic question is the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and the data centers needed to support it. Investment in AI has helped fuel economic growth, Stevenson said, but that growth hasn't necessarily translated into more jobs or higher wages for American workers. Although constructing data centers can create jobs in the short term, Stevenson said the facilities provide relatively few permanent positions once completed. Instead, she suggested Michigan should focus on attracting companies and industries capable of sustaining employment for decades."You know what some of those San Francisco companies should do? They should relocate to Detroit," Stevenson said.With new leadership preparing to take office in Lansing and Washington, Stevenson said the challenge will be turning voters' demands for economic stability into policies that create lasting opportunities.Scroll up to listen the full conversation, or read the transcript below:April Baer: What a big flex the election was for the power of pocketbook issues this week, as voters in Michigan and elsewhere expressed a tsunami-sized wish for change. The stock market has been up and down like a yo-yo this week, with election-driven surges of investor confidence followed by losses for stocks that are tied to the build-out of AI data centers.Also, what now? Will new Democratic leaders wish to rein in Trump's excesses, reach the factors that have made life less predictable and more expensive in Michigan?With me now is Betsey Stevenson, a professor of public policy and economics at the University of Michigan's Ford School. She is also a former chief economist for the U.S. Department of Labor.Betsey, welcome back to Stateside. Great to have you.Betsey Stevenson: Great to talk with you.AB: So, through an economic lens, what is your read on this? How much of the vote and the blue wave nationwide had to do with the economy and the way we all experience it?BS: Well, you know, I want to start by pointing out that the Republicans, for decades, many, many decades, have had the upper hand with voters when it comes to trust over managing the economy. You ask people, who do you think is going to do a better job with the economy? And, you know, voters were more likely to say Republicans.And frankly, that continued even when there wasn't really a lot of good economic evidence that Republicans were actually better for the economy. For many decades, you know, Republicans often did things that were harmful to the economy, but they still maintained a belief with voters.And what happened was that belief has been cracked. And in fact, we saw that in survey data in 2026, when you started to see voters and Americans more generally saying that they think Democrats have an edge in handling the economy.So that's the first step, was that they now believe Democrats will do better with the economy. And that was a really tough nut for Democrats to crack, to be able to convince voters that they could do it.AB: We know that the agenda for many of the newly elected congressional reps and senators, Abdul El-Sayed, people like Sean McCann in the Michigan House delegation, they've talked a lot about trying to address some of these economic factors on the campaign trail.But also, we know that there is a hunger among Dems in D.C. to try to rein in a president who's consistently pushed back on the boundaries of executive authority, maybe look at some of the leaders who are part of the Trump cabinet.If you're newly elected, what problems would you say voters want to fix first from that economic standpoint?BS: I think you are laying out that there's two things that voters are asking for. One is more accountability, and the other one is just basic pocketbook kitchen table issues. Like, are we, you know, can you bring prices down or at least slow the rate of increase of prices?I think that's what they're asking for. The biggest risk Democrats have is they get distracted by the accountability and they go too far to trying to hold people accountable.I think the first step, what I would do and what I recommend Democrats newly elected do, if you're elected on pocketbook issues, Congress has the power of the purse, and you need to take that back. And that means the first thing that any newly elected person should do when they're sworn in in early January is reassert Congress's power to tax and spend.And by doing that, they can show that, first of all, Congress matters. Even if they've got Trump there ready to veto it, I think that voters will still reward Democrats if they're out there passing bills that say end the president's ability to impose tariffs. So they get rid of the tariffs. They're going to show that they are doing something to try to bring prices down.If they do what they, you know, a very first step thing would be to put the subsidies back for the ACA. Americans have seen an enormous increase in the cost of health insurance, and that cost has come really from two direct things Republicans did: got rid of the subsidies and have had cuts to Medicaid. They can reverse those things immediately.And then, of course, they need to try to check the president's war powers and see if they can bring the Iran war to, you know, a reasonable close so that we can get some stability in oil prices.Those four things are really the immediate things that show that they're addressing pocketbook issues. And I think the risk is the distraction of there's so much corruption that they've been witnessing in D.C. articles.content: Stephen Miller, at the time White House deputy chief of staff, and former press secretary Karoline Leavitt speak to reporters at the White House briefing on May 1, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump announced Friday he will elevate Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, the first shake-up of his administration officials since Democrats trounced Republicans in the midterms. Former Chief of Staff Susie Wiles will move to the “Trump Political Operation,” the president announced in an afternoon post on his Truth Social platform. Trump said Miller, a key figure behind the administration’s aggressive mass deportation campaign, is “one of my most trusted advisors.” The president told reporters outside the White House that he wants Miller to “just run things well.” “Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it, very good politically, and he’s a very good manager. He’ll do a great job,” he said. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries slammed the move, writing on X Friday that Miller “is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands.” “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today,” Jeffries, who is poised to become House speaker in January, wrote on X. Blue wave The move comes after voters rebuked Trump Tuesday, giving Democrats sizable majorities in both the House and Senate this coming Congress. In a backlash to Trump, Hispanics who voted for the president in 2024 shunned him in the midterms. Every voter demographic sharply swung toward Democrats, but Latinos shifted sharply, by 21 points, according to an analysis by NPR, and a separate analysis by The Associated Press. Miller has been a proponent of the Trump administration’s campaign against birthright citizenship, which it lost in a major case at the U.S. Supreme Court. In an interview with Fox News host Will Cain in December 2025, Miller described birthright citizenship as “the greatest scam in history.” “With a lot of these immigrant groups, not only is the first generation unsuccessful. Again, Somalia is a clear example here,” he said. “You see persistent issues in every subsequent generation. So you see consistent high rates of welfare use, consistent high rates of criminal activity, consistent failures to assimilate.” The claim that immigrants commit more crimes than other demographics in the United States is unfounded, according to several studies of national crime statistics compiled by the Migration Policy Institute. The institute found that immigrants in the U.S. commit crimes at lower rates than the U.S.-born population. The New York Times, reporting those comments by Miller, said that studies have documented the upward mobility of immigrant children and that experts questioned his underlying arguments. The liberal-leaning Brookings Institution has reported that “immigrants are a fiscal boon to the U.S.” and that “Empirical evidence indicates that immigrants have historically contributed more in tax revenue than they receive in public benefits, creating a substantial fiscal surplus for the U.S. government over time.” During that same interview, Miller blamed immigrants in the United States for low test scores and healthcare costs, among other issues. 2026 deadly surge Miller also advocated for the surge of immigration agents into mostly Democrat-led American cities throughout 2026, and did not back down after extreme instances of violence. In January after federal agents fatally shot Alex Pretti in Minnesota, Miller reposted a video of the killing posted by the Democratic National Committee on X with the comments: “A would-be assassin tried to murder federal law enforcement and the official Democrat account sides with the terrorists.” Miller steered immigration policies during Trump’s first term. He has been a fixture of Trump’s political apparatus for a decade, and played a role in Trump’s successful presidential campaign beginning in 2015.

Earth's churning mantle may have created the Great Unconformity
articles.description: Explaining the Great Unconformity, where Cambrian deposits sit on top of older rocks.
articles.content: In the Grand Canyon, there is a line in the rock where time seems to have gone missing. Ancient crystalline rocks mark its bottom, while sandstones laid down as life started to diversify during the Cambrian explosion mark the top. “It’s called the Great Unconformity, and it’s a gap in the geologic record,” says Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, Australia. "This gap can be anywhere between 200 million years, which is not that impressive, to more than a billion years.” In a recent Nature study, Flament and his colleague Santosh Dhungana argue that this gap was carved with help from deep within the planet. According to their models, slow currents of hot rock in Earth's mantle pushed entire continents up for hundreds of millions of years, letting glaciers grind them down and then let them sink, allowing fresh sediments to bury the scar. The largest hole in the rock record might be a fingerprint of processes happening deep in the planet's interior. Ice and sea The oldest sediments resting on the Great Unconformity in North America are between 635 and 482 million years old. Geologists have traced it across most of North America and parts of northern Europe and northern China. “Something seems to have happened, in particular in North America,” Flament says.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Another Detroit concrete crusher? Sir Crush-A-Lot draws neighborhood opposition
articles.description: DVM Utilities, Inc. began operating last fall in northwest Detroit with a state permit but without required city permits. It halted operations this year after a complaint was made to the city and DVM became aware it needed a permit.
articles.content: A Macomb County utility contractor is seeking approval to locate its first concrete crusher at an industrial park in Detroit near a residential neighborhood. DVM Utilities, Inc. began operating Sir-Crush-A-Lot off I-96 and Evergreen in northwest Detroit in fall 2025 with a state permit but without required city permits. It halted operations earlier this year after a complaint was made to the city and DVM became aware it needed a city permit. During a special land use hearing on Wednesday, Detroit’s Buildings, Safety Engineering, and Environmental Department (BSEED) considered DVM’s application to “establish a very high-impact manufacturing or processing facility” on a 3.67-acre site zoned for heavy industry. One neighboring business spoke in support, and BSEED received 190 letters in opposition, staff noted at the hearing, with concerns mostly focused on air quality impacts. The crusher would be located in the Jeffries Schoolcraft Industrial Park, within a quarter mile from residents and two miles from an existing concrete crusher. Kevin McDonald, director of operations for Sterling Heights-based DVM Utilities, said he thought the company was fully permitted after receiving authorization from the state, and didn’t know it needed a city permit to operate. DVM was founded in 1981 and provides above-and below-ground utility infrastructure services. “We want to be in full compliance, we’re not trying to do anything backhanded,” he said at the virtual hearing. Related: Detroit could block billionaire-owned concrete plant from further neighborhood expansion How Detroit ceded a historically Black neighborhood to a billionaire-owned concrete facility Under settlement, company can’t open new concrete crushers in Detroit Detroit and Salem residents struggle to ‘coexist’ with concrete crushers. Is Wayne prepared? Following recommendations from city departments that testified at the hearing, BSEED Director Dave Bell will make a decision. If the permit is denied, DVM can appeal to the Board of Zoning Appeals. The concrete crusher is not the first in Detroit to begin operations without proper city permitting. In recent years, truck traffic and dust from another concrete site nearby, Dino-Mite, upset neighbors and prompted legal action. And, in Cadillac Heights, near the original Buddy’s Pizza, another company began mixing concrete in 2022 without city permits. The Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) issued DVM the permit to crush concrete in April 2025. That fall, Sir-Crush-A-Lot crushed 1,115 tons of concrete and used 2,300 gallons of water, according to company records submitted to the state. DVM first applied for a permit with the city in April 2026, following an inspection driven by a complaint, according to BSEED spokesperson Georgette Johnson. Sir-Crush-A-Lot has received material from the demolition of the old Wayne County Jail that it hopes to crush and reuse. Credit: Jena Brooker Piles of material were found during the April inspection, but the company was not in operation, said Johnson and several tickets were issued to DVM for not having the required documentation. “They were found responsible by default, and they paid all the tickets,” she said by email. EGLE spokesperson Josef Stephens said by email on Friday that the department tries “to remind people that they may need other permissions; however, it is the company’s responsibility to ensure they have all necessary permits, licenses, etc., prior to starting operation.” The site has received material from the old Wayne County Jail, among others, according to DVM representatives. Detroit City Planner Dolores Perales-Lara asked during the Wednesday hearing about the need for another concrete crusher, given Dino-Mite is located nearby. Engineering and environmental and health partners for DVM noted during the hearing that concrete crushing is “an integral part to all construction in the city of Detroit” and said that it’s good news for everyone that Detroit is undergoing so much development. Major construction has reshaped the city in the years since Detroit’s bankruptcy, with the first new skyscraper in 50 years, new hotels, sports complexes and new sidewalks, which all require concrete. A DVM representative noted during the hearing that concrete crushing is “an integral part to all construction in the city of Detroit.” Crushing concrete allows material to be recycled and reused for new projects, and it diverts the material from the landfill. However, when crushed, the concrete can release dust particles that can be harmful to human health. Four years ago, residents fought a similar fight: an asphalt company wanted to build a plant just on the other side of the highway from the Sir-Crush-A-Lot site. Matthew Milia lives in nearby Rosedale Park, suffers from asthma, and has a 3-year-old. He told DVM during the hearing that he took issue with the company using Detroit’s renewal to demonstrate the need. “That rationale does nothing to justify the location for this deleterious public health hazard,” he said. Neighbors have been working hard to revitalize the area, he said. A quarter-mile away is nonprofit community farm Foster Patch. Stoepel Park, which features recreational sports fields, a playground, and other amenities, is within a mile. And soon, Faust Haus will build a new coffee roastery in the area. “This is just way too close to major residential centers, public parks, and our own backyards, where our children are growing up to make any sort of sense for the community,” said Milia. Nonprofit Foster Patch Community Garden is located approximately a quarter of a mile from the site of Sir-Crush-A-Lot. Credit: Jena Brooker, BridgeDetroit The state environmental permit was issued after EGLE employee Matt Heintz inspected the site in April 2025 and found that it met requirements to crush concrete. It’s at least 500 feet from residents and commercial buildings, located in an area zoned for industry right by the highway, and DVM had plans to use water to mitigate dust, Heintz noted. Originally, the company proposed its crusher operation for a site in the city of Inkster, but it would be “too close to residential,” Heintz wrote in the same report. Mark Javor, managing director of Metro Welding Supply, a business adjacent to the Sir-Crush-A-Lot site, spoke on Wednesday in support of the company. “They’ve been really easy to work with, very quick to react since they moved in,” he said. Javor also has a property adjacent to Dino-Mite, which is about two miles from Sir-Crush-A-Lot. Dino-Mite has been in an ongoing fight with residents for spreading dust into the neighborhood and has received hundreds of city tickets for dust. BSEED sought to shut it down, sparking a multi-year legal battle which ended with a settlement requiring the company to step up efforts to reduce dust. Although the two concrete operations are unrelated, many opponents at the Wednesday hearing brought up Dino-Mite, sharing concerns that Sir-Crush-A-Lot could have a similar impact. McDonald on Wednesday said the comparison was unfair. “The equipment that we’re using is more modern, probably than, again, the other place, the other concrete crushing place that continues to be discussed and for us to be compared to, which is unfair,” he said. McDonald estimated several thousand tons of concrete would be crushed per year at the Detroit site. However, the state permit authorizes Sir-Crush-A-Lot to process up to 2 million tons of concrete a year. Dino-Mite is permitted to crush 600,000 tons. DVM said Wednesday that its BSEED permit application is crafted to meet city requirements, including installing two air monitors to ensure compliance with air quality standards. Upon hearing resident concerns during Wednesday’s hearing, company officials said they would engage with the community and install as many air monitors as residents wanted, provide a tipline for residents to report drivers on unauthorized roads, or other measures. “We’re going to do everything we need to do, and more as needed to be a good neighbor,” McDonald said. State Sen. Mary Cavanagh, D-Redford Township, who represents the neighborhood, said she was disappointed that BSEED is considering the permit application. “I’m in complete opposition, and I really think that we can’t keep risking the health of our community members and ask to please deny this application as I work at the state level to make sure that we don’t increase environmental outputs to our beautiful populations,” she said. Lead staff attorney at the Sugar Law Center for Economic and Social Justice, Liz Jacob, said it would be unjust to add pollution to the neighborhood, given the area’s “burden” already. The neighborhood, she said, is exposed to more air pollution than 90% of the entire state of Michigan, according to the United States Environmental Protection Agency. “We cannot keep sacrificing the health of our Detroiters,” she said.

Former Trump White House chief of staff Mark Meadows reacts to Stephen Miller replacing Susie Wiles
articles.content: Stephen Miller has been one of Donald Trump’s most influential and longest-serving advisers. Here are five things to know about his background, his role in shaping immigration policy and his influence inside the White House. President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, installing as his closest adviser a loyal, combative bulldog for his “America First” agenda as the president prepares to stare down a newly empowered Democratic Congress next year. Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s longest-serving aides, joining his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He most recently has served as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy. Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10. The staff shuffle signals that Trump, whose Republican Party was handed monumental defeats in Tuesday's midterm elections, is resisting a conciliatory approach to Democratic lawmakers who are eager to investigate the administration — including Miller himself as a top target. Miller, 41, is a dogged defender of Trump and has built a deep and sophisticated understanding of a president's executive power and how the federal government operates, portending a potential burst of executive actions in the final two years of Trump's presidency. Wiles gave Trump her resignation on Thursday night, a person familiar with the events told the Associated Press, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization. Trump on Friday night denied that he made the change because he was unhappy with his team after the deep losses his party suffered. “Not because of the election. It’s just time," Trump said. "Sometimes you change. The election wasn’t my election. I wasn’t on the ballot.” Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term. “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement. She added that her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change. The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026. During the midterm campaign, Miller took frequent partisan swipes at Democrats, calling them “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” on social media and promoted unfounded theories about election fraud in California and Alaska. He has been a major part of the Trump administration’s anti-fraud task force targeting benefit programs and a decision to suspend Microsoft and others from a green card program. He also served as homeland security adviser at the White House, giving him a perch from which to coordinate with other agencies across the government. He joined Trump on Friday for his trip to Florida, and the president noted to reporters that "Stephen has been with me from the beginning. "He gets it; very good politically," Trump said as he departed the White House. "He’ll do a great job. Great manager.” But the immigration policies that Miller is so closely allied with were a major liability for Republicans during the just-wrapped election. The midterm AP Voter Poll found that most voters, about 6 in 10, said the administration’s immigration enforcement actions had gone too far and that they “somewhat” or “strongly” disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement had handled its responsibilities. “Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” said Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become chairman of the powerful House Oversight Committee. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.” In a statement, Garcia added: “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.” Trump on Friday praised Wiles, the veteran Florida operative who joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid, as having done a “very good job, great job.” But he added, “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.” Wiles, 69, is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager. She has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term. Wiles stuck with the job even after her breast cancer diagnosis. Deep into the midterm campaign, six months after having revealed her diagnosis, she said she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear. In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable. Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd. In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ’ successful run for governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024. But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff. The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.” Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who, in turn, disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” though she did not deny making the comments. In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.” “I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.” Associated Press writers Michelle L. Price in West Palm Beach, Florida and Jill Colvin in New York contributed to this report.
