articles.content: While you might be pondering whether to replace a smartphone with one that has a slightly better camera or a second screen, the Federal Aviation Administration is planning a much bigger leap in technology for the country's air traffic control system. The FAA said yesterday that it will stop using floppy disks as part of a long-awaited upgrade that will give air traffic controllers faster access to data needed for crucial safety alerts. The new Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) will be installed in 435 facilities, replacing several information display systems dating to the 1980s. The FAA "is continuing its historic modernization of America’s air traffic control system by replacing outdated floppy disks that contain vital weather and other critical information with a streamlined, 21st-century system," the agency said. E-IDS will be "deployed to operational control positions at more than 400 facilities across all air traffic control domains," and "provide operationally essential information for controlling aircraft," the FAA said.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Monroe policy renews debate about trans athletes in Michigan schools
articles.description: A Monroe Public Schools policy that blocks transgender girls from participating on its girls sports teams renews concern and legal questions about the civil rights of student athletes.
articles.content: LANSING – A recent decision by the Monroe Public Schools Board of Education to restrict participation in girls’ sports based on sex assigned at birth has renewed discussion about how Michigan schools handle transgender athletes and the legal questions surrounding their policies. Andrew Shaw is superintendent of Monroe Public Schools. (Courtesy of Monroe Public School) Superintendent Andrew Shaw said in a statement, “The policy that was approved is for Monroe Public Schools only and does not impact any visiting school.” The decision comes as school officials statewide and nationally continue to navigate questions surrounding transgender student participation in athletics. The Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA), which governs interscholastic sports for member schools, currently reviews eligibility for transgender girls on a case-by-case basis. According to its handbook, eligibility decisions may consider school records, medical documentation and other information related to a student’s gender identity and transition. While Monroe’s new policy bases participation in girls’ sports on sex assigned at birth, the association’s current policy evaluates transgender athletes individually rather than imposing a blanket restriction. The MHSAA policy does not prohibit girls from participating on boys’ teams. Therefore, it does not participate in matters involving transgender boy (female to male) student-athletes on boys’ teams. Transgender girls (male to female) seeking to participate in state tournament competitions are subject to an eligibility review by the association’s executive director. Association officials say its policies are designed to comply with state and federal law. Related: GOP slams ‘woke’ politics, bathroom signs as Monroe college tax vote nears Monroe County became Trump country. Rising costs could test that loyalty Out of reach: Where do Michigan’s trans youth go for care now? “For many years, (MHSAA) policy in this area has been crafted to be fully compliant with federal and state law,” said Geoff Kimmerly, its communications director “We believe the claims made are legally unsound, and we will defend that position through the legal process.”Donate Kimmerly declined further comment, citing an ongoing federal lawsuit against Monroe Public Schools, its athletic director and its superintendent over the circumstances of, and in response to, a transgender athlete playing on a visiting volleyball team. The debate extends beyond Michigan. Voters in Colorado, Washington, Nebraska and Arizona passed ballot measures related to transgender youth rights on Election Day, including proposals involving school sports participation and gender-affirming care. Missouri voters defeated a proposal to ban gender-affirming care. The measures marked the first general election in which voters in multiple states were asked directly to weigh in on policies affecting transgender youth. More than two dozen Republican-led states, including neighboring Indiana and Ohio, have adopted bans on transgender girls participating in girls’ sports. Those laws were upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in June. The issue also intersects with Michigan’s Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act. That law prohibits discrimination on the basis of religion, race, color, national origin, age, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and marital status in places of public accommodation and public services. Under the law, individuals may not be denied the full and equal enjoyment of services or facilities because of their gender identity or expression. Jay Kaplan, an attorney with the ACLU of Michigan’s LGBTQ+ Project, said policies restricting participation based on sex assigned at birth conflict with those protections. Jay Kaplan is the LGBTQ+ Project attorney at the ACLU of Michigan. (Courtesy of ACLU of Michigan) “Our state civil rights law explicitly covers gender identity and gender expression,” Kaplan said. “You can’t discriminate in terms of providing the same opportunities and ability to participate in educational programs.” Kaplan said transgender students often participate in athletics for the same reasons as other students. “They want to be part of a team. They want to participate in competition with their team. They want to expand their skills,” he said. Kaplan also noted that the MHSSA already evaluates transgender girls seeking to compete in girls’ sports through an individualized waiver process. “They do an individualized assessment of that student to look at the potential issue of competitive advantage before granting a waiver,” he said. Kaplan said policies like Monroe’s could have broader effects on transgender students beyond athletics. “It sends a message that they’re less than, that they’re other, that they’re not entitled to the same rights and opportunities,” Kaplan said. This story was originally published by the Capital News Service.

articles.title: Lawsuits challenge Money Out of Politics ballot measure on First Amendment grounds
articles.description: Two lawsuits have been filed against Proposal 2, the “Michiganders for Money Out of Politics” ballot measure that passed on Tuesday with over 80% of the vote, arguing it violates the First Amendment. The proposal is scheduled to take effect by Dec. 3, 2026, under Michigan election law, unless a court blocks its implementation. The […]
articles.content: Getty ImagesTwo lawsuits have been filed against Proposal 2, the “Michiganders for Money Out of Politics” ballot measure that passed on Tuesday with over 80% of the vote, arguing it violates the First Amendment. The proposal is scheduled to take effect by Dec. 3, 2026, under Michigan election law, unless a court blocks its implementation. The measure bans campaign spending from “regulated electric and gas utilities, contractors with over $250,000 annually in government contracts, and people and organizations with substantial connections to those utilities or contractors.” Both lawsuits — one filed by the Mackinac Center for Public Policy and the other filed by CMS Energy, Consumers Energy and DTE — were filed in federal court in the Western District of Michigan. Both lawsuits question whether the state can restrict political spending by utilities and their employees based on their contributions to the elected officials who regulate them. The Mackinac Center, a free-market policy think tank, writes in its lawsuit, “It is an alarming and far-reaching law. It also violates the First Amendment.” Christy McGillivray, executive director of Voters Not Politicians and a co-chair of the ballot effort, speaks to supporters in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026 after The Associated Press called the race for the “yes” vote. (Screenshot) Specifically, that suit challenges the portions of the law related to “Electioneering Communications” and “Campaign Expenditures,” arguing that the text of the law that Proposal 2 enacted is too broad in defining which organizations would be subject to significant reporting requirements of their donors and contributions under the new law. “Mackinac has no way of determining which of its public communications will qualify as supporting, promoting, attacking, or opposing a candidate or ballot question under Proposal 2, as this broad phrase could include virtually every statement made about those subjects,” the lawsuit writes. “Mackinac likewise has no way of determining which communications will qualify as being made ‘for the purpose of influencing or attempting to influence the action of the voters.’ Mackinac will thus be required to either refrain from speech that could fit these vague standards or face the burdensome reporting requirements that apply to political committees.” They argue that this is a First Amendment violation in limiting the free speech rights of the Mackinac Center because, “The reporting requirements burden Mackinac’s ability to engage in constitutionally protected speech by imposing onerous costs on Mackinac and exposing it and its supporters to harassment. This creates an impermissible chilling effect on Mackinac’s speech and association.” “Michiganders shouldn’t face fines or jail just so that they can discuss politicians, policy, or elections,” said Patrick J. Wright, vice president of the Mackinac Center Legal Foundation, in a press release announcing the lawsuit. “These rules threaten access to information voters rely on and violate the privacy of people who support organizations they believe in. We’re bringing this lawsuit to protect free speech and open debate and to prevent giving partisans a nasty tool that can be used to criminally punish their opponents for daring to speak their minds.” The lawsuit from CMS, Consumers and DTE, on the other hand, argues that the First Amendment is violated by Proposal 2 through “speaker-based viewpoint discrimination” in specifically targeting utility companies and their employees. Even if treated as content-neutral, the lawsuit continues on, the law fails to meet the threshold needed to limit campaign contributions, which would be “preventing quid pro quo corruption or its appearance.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE “There is no evidence of such corruption by Michigan’s utilities—no scandal, no exchange of official acts for money, no examples whatsoever,” lawyers for the utility companies wrote, adding that the coalition of organizations behind the MMOP ballot measure have “regularly opposed Michigan’s utilities” on policy issues. Samuel Bagenstos, a University of Michigan law professor and lawyer for the ballot measure, however, was confident that the defense in court of the new law would be strong, adding that new campaign finance laws regularly trigger lawsuits, but that the proposal was drafted with existing judicial decisions in mind. Maura Cowley, the campaign manager for the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics campaign, said the lawsuit was “no surprise.” “The corporations bankrolling our opposition have been gearing up for this lawsuit since Proposal 2 first qualified for the ballot, if not before,” Cowley wrote. “On Tuesday, Michiganders spoke loud and clear, voting to pass Proposal 2 with an overwhelming majority and delivering a resounding mandate to end pay-to-play politics and put power back where it belongs – with the people. The bottom line is that we are confident Proposal 2 will withstand legal scrutiny, and we were fully expecting and are prepared to take on this and any challenge.”

articles.title: Trump’s arch is blocked for now, but a glitzy new website highlights the plans
articles.description: Trump’s arch is blocked for now, but a glitzy new website highlights the plans AP News Judge Promptly Blocks Work on Trump’s Triumphal Arch After It’s Approved The New York Times White House recasts Trump arch as military tribute Reuters Judge blocks Trump’s arch after panel approves construction Politico Judge halts construction of Trump's arch. And, Labor Department to release jobs report NPR
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal court has temporarily blocked President Donald Trump from breaking ground for his towering memorial arch, but that hasn’t stopped his administration from pushing forward with the plans for building it, starting with a glitzy new website launched Friday. The site’s debut is yet another sign of how much Trump is leaning into his efforts to make over the White House and Washington to his own gilded tastes, even after his party lost control of Congress in a midterm-election drubbing. It was the fourth day this week alone that the administration promoted his projects. The website declares that the 250-foot (76-meter) structure — which is slated to rise in a mass of blindingly gold ornamentation and stately gray granite between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery — will be formally known as the United States Military Triumphal Arch. Describing the arch as “an American vision finally realized,” the site offers bird’s-eye views of the proposal from many angles and shows off the declarations it will feature: “One Nation Under God” on one side and “Golden Age of America” on another. It’s also set to have towering gold doors complete with panels of sculptures at its base. At its very top, the structure features a golden-hued cherub hoisting a flaming torch that recalls a smaller version of the Statue of Liberty. The website does not say how much the project will cost or how it will be paid for, although some estimates have reached as high as $100 million. The White House highlighted the website the morning after U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order that prohibits work on the site for 14 days. That order followed a vote to approve the arch by a federal planning commission that is stocked with Trump’s allies. With Democrats taking control of Congress in January, Trump’s renovation projects will encounter far more scrutiny and roadblocks — from his effort to put his own name on the Kennedy Center to remaking a public golf course and building his massive White House ballroom and the arch. The president on Monday focused his final remarks before the midterm elections talking up his costly and problem-plagued effort to overhaul the Lincoln Memorial’s Reflecting Pool. The day after the losses, on Wednesday, he took reporters on a tour of the ballroom’s construction site. And his first official action after his party lost control of Congress was to declare, on Thursday, that the Oval Office would become a national monument. The arch website features the word “Triumph” in gold cursive script recalling the typeface used at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida and similar flourishes that have been affixed to the White House as part of his overhaul of the Oval Office and West Wing. The arch plans feature an event space in the horizontal part of the structure reached by elevators and stairs. But inside its “massive columns will be storage for munitions,” the site states, as well as areas on the pedestal and observation deck that will be “set aside for snipers, countersnipers, and provisions for a sniper nest.” An open ground area at the monument’s base “will be designed for launching drones and other homeland security assets,” the site says, while also noting that the arch “will be Highly Secretive but, at the same time, a Top Level and Lethal structure, the likes of which has not been seen in this Country before.” “It is long overdue, and has been sought for many years, especially by the Military,” it says. Trump has said for months that the monument would be inspired by the Arc de Triomphe in Paris and that Washington has wanted a similar structure for centuries — even though that’s not true. He previously joked that it might be called the “Arc de Trump.” The website repeats Trump’s inaccurate claims. It also features a picture of the president and quotes him as saying, “This will be the greatest and most beautiful triumphal arch, anywhere in the world.”

articles.title: What Michigan's triumph over UConn means for women's basketball team's chances in March
articles.description: An evolving Michigan women's basketball team under coach Kim Barnes Arico shows defiance in a win over one of the nation’s best.
articles.content: The NCAA's No. 2 and No. 5 teams clash at Crisler Center.(Paul Sancya / Associated Press)The 5th-ranked Michigan women's basketball team notched a huge win last night, beating perennial juggernaut UConn, the No. 2 team in the county, 77-66 on Thursday night at Crisler Center. The victory lit up hopes for a Final Four appearance, with a powerhouse class of juniors – and talent to spare.With point guard Mila Holloway out with an injury, it was not entirely clear the Wolverines would have what was necessary to take on Geno Auriemma’s squad. But U-M held on, despite some shooting problems, to pull away in the fourth quarter.Detroit Free Press sports columnist Shawn Windsor spoke with Stateside host April Baer about the win and its significance.This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.April Baer: This game may not have been the cleanest one the Wolverines ever played, but with a ten-point margin on the win … Shawn, would you call that decisive?Shawn Windsor: Well, they pulled away really late, I don't know that I would call it decisive. I would call it an impressive win. It was a confident win. And what was different for Michigan this time – because they've played several top-ranked teams the last couple of years and have come up just short – they made the plays right that they needed to make, [the plays] they haven't been able to make. And when UConn made a couple of runs, Michigan answered every time. And that felt different.Baer: The team that coach (Kim) Barnes Arico has is built around some very strong talents. Mila Holloway, of course, was out with an injury, but it didn't seem like the Wolverines were lacking last night. You know, Syla Swords was there. Olivia Olson, contributing some real star shots. Te’Yala Delfosse really picked up some slack in the third quarter. And these are athletes who've been playing together now since their freshman year. Have you had a chance to notice anything as they've developed together?Windsor: There are a few things. First of all, Geno Auriemma, the legendary UConn coach, who's the best coach in college women's basketball – he was saying last night that when you're building a program, the hardest thing to do is to convince that first really good class to come to you, [to] convince them that they're going to be the ones that are going to turn it around. It's human nature – so many high schoolers want to go maybe to an established program and, and be part of something and develop and get on to Europe and play or the WNBA. What's interesting about this class is that now, while Kim Barnes has had some success, she's never had a group quite like this. Olivia Olson and Syla Swords in particular, they were both five-star, highly regarded recruits. To get them to believe and to come to Ann Arbor was the first step. And they and they did, and they've all stayed. And Coach Barnes said again last night after the win that, “Hey, my gals could have gone anywhere. A lot of schools would have been happy to play them. But they they believe what we're doing here and they stay.” Delfosse, in particular, looks like a different player. She's always been talented, but she was a two-way menace last night. And if this is their trajectory, then they're going to have a chance to do something really interesting in the spring, for sure. A near-capacity crowd as Crisler Center roared as Michigan pulled ahead of UConn in the third quarter.(April Baer / Michigan Public)Baer: I do need to talk about the shooting. Some of the shooting from the line. And also, layups didn't go the way that that they should have gone. Can we can trust the team has a pattern of fixing the problems as they come up through the season?Windsor: Absolutely. We can see the development of the group of juniors and how much better they've gotten year over year. There were yeah, there were a few layups that were just completely uncontested, where nobody else was around. I would chalk a little bit of that up to the opponent, the first game of the season. I would say that's going to get a little bit better.Baer: UConn's coach, Geno Auriemma, was talking in his postgame press conference, giving big coach dad vibes. He wasn't mad. He was just disappointed! He felt his team had tried to lean on its stars to make up the deficit when UConn got into trouble. I couldn't help but wonder how these teams might match up again in the postseason. Do you have thoughts?Windsor: I do, I think it would be similar. [UConn has the] reigning player of the year – arguably the best player in college women's basketball. Sarah Strong picked up her third foul and missed, really, the second quarter. And I would imagine that would make a difference in a rematch. On the other hand, Michigan's missing their starting point guard, Mila Holloway, I don't know if she would be back for a rematch that could potentially make a difference. But Michigan's got some depth as Coach Arico pointed out last night. It's not just the Olivia Olson and Syla Swords right there. They've got a lot. They can get shots from lots of different places. They can get plays. They have playmaking in lots of different places, and it's going to make them tough to tough to guard. I would imagine they'd be able to stick with them if they meet again in March.

articles.description: Stuntman/director Chad Stahelski and 87Eleven bring us an action-packed dystopian, futuristic thriller.
articles.content: Those of us missing the John Wick universe can take heart, because Chad Stahelski—who created that franchise—is coming back early next year with a new dystopian action film. It's called Karōshi (a Japanese term that means "death overwork"), and Lionsgate released a killer trailer that puts this film at the top of my list of "must see" movies of 2027. Dying from working too hard is a very real phenomenon, not just in Japan and much of Asia, but also in Sweden. The physical cause is usually stress-related heart attacks or strokes, as well as suicide (karōjisatsu in Japan). Writer/director Takashi Doscher has transported that concept to a grim, futuristic corporate Manhattan, specifically a company called Ikigai Technologies. Per the official premise: Karōshi is an action-thriller set in a near-future Manhattan, where corporate loyalty and cultural tradition have reshaped everyday life. When a mysterious outsider infiltrates a powerful company after a worker’s death, he exposes the violent system hidden beneath its polished surface. Teo Yoo (Past Lives) stars as the aptly named Hiro, who is clearly out for vengeance against the offending corporation. The cast also includes Takehiro Hira, so memorable in the 2024 miniseries Shōgun, as well as Giancarlo Esposito, Cynthia Erivo, Bill Camp, Richard Harmon, Isabel May, and Show Kasamatsu.Read full article Comments

articles.title: All the ways Michigan made history in the 2026 midterm election
articles.description: There were historic firsts and a blue wave all over the country. Here's what happened in Michigan and what it means for the next two years.
articles.content: (Kalloli Bhatt / Canva)Hi! You’re reading the It’s Just Politics newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the It's Just Politics podcast for all the political news you need each week.Last week, I said I would be watching Saginaw County on election night to see whether it aligned with race outcomes, much like it has in past presidential elections. Well, it did. Not only did Saginaw County shift blue, so largely did the nation.Tuesday’s election had some historic wins around the country.This election had a record-breaking number of women running for state and federal offices. New Mexico elected Deb Haaland, the first Native American female governor; Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota became the first Native U.S. Senator; Keisha Lance Bottoms is set to be Georgia’s first Black female governor; and, last but not least, Michigan elected the first Muslim Senator, Abdul El-Sayed.Michigan makes history, tooApart from El-Sayed, Michigan also elected:Jeremy Moss, our first openly gay member of CongressSean McCann, our first tribal member of CongressJoanna Whaley, our first openly transgender woman legislatorJocelyn Benson and Winnie Brinks, our first all-female governor and lieutenant governor ticketThese historic victories happened during a wider Democratic shift, including changes in Michigan’s congressional delegation and state government.Across the country, Democrats made gains in Congress, gubernatorial races and state legislatures. Michigan was part of that shift, becoming one of five states that gained Democratic trifectas.Is this trifecta different?In the new year, Democrats will hold the governor, attorney general and secretary of state seats, as well as having majorities in both the Michigan House and Senate.We’ve been here before. In the 2023-24 legislative term, to be exact.“Democratic lawmakers passed many marquee laws during their first year in complete power, like gun safety policies, clean energy standards, and repealing anti-union legislation,” reports Michigan Public Radio Network’s Colin Jackson. “But many felt like they left too much on the table during a slow 2024. Republicans retook the House of Representatives that year.”It is important to note that this time around, Democrats have more than a one-vote majority, giving this trifecta different implications than last time. It not only gives Democrats more leniency on individual defections, but also allows them to advance legislation without needing as much bipartisan support.That space could help Democrats pass some of Governor-Elect Jocelyn Benson’s more ambitious policies, such as prioritizing unity, economic growth and public schools.And ambitious they’ll need to be. Our first all-female ticket is inheriting a state that has low test scores, a housing and health care affordability problem and an ambiguous direction when it comes to data centers.It’s unknown just how Benson will accomplish her goals, even with a favorable Legislature. Some, like her plan to pass a $5,000 caregiver tax credit, are expensive. Others, like her proposal to protect and expand Medicaid, are more dependent on federal policies, which are outside of Benson’s control.What’s ahead for MichiganNone of that is to say that Benson will never have help from Congress.Tuesday’s blue wave also gave Democrats a majority in both chambers of Congress, meaning they could pass legislation that they say would ease burdens on states and voters. It also seems President Donald Trump could be willing to work with this new cohort, though he may use his veto power.This new, historic majority ushers a variety of diverse voices from diverse backgrounds into the legislative process. Congress has changed and Michigan’s representation in Congress has changed too.The real question is how much these newly-elected officials, in Congress and Michigan, will be able to accomplish in the next two years.Until next week,Kalloli Bhatt, Digital Content Producer_______________________Have questions about Michigan politics? Or, just want to let us know what you want more of (less of?) in the newsletter? We always want to hear from you! Shoot us an email at politics@michiganpublic.org!_____________________________________________________________________More Political News_______________________Today’s newsletter was written and produced by Kalloli Bhatt, and edited by Michelle Keller.

articles.title: Fleeing driver ordered to higher court in Clinton Twp. double-fatal crash
articles.content: A 55-year-old Sterling Heights man was ordered Thursday to appear in the higher trial court on two counts of second-degree murder and other charges for a crash that killed two young men earlier this year in Clinton Township. Keith Lamar Blackwell was bound over to Macomb County Circuit Court by Judge Sebastian Lucido of 41B District Court following a preliminary examination on the murder charges, two counts of first-degree fleeing police and two counts of reckless driving causing death for the March 2026 incident that killed Richard Talley, 23, of Roseville, and Joshua Jones, 24, of Southfield. “Two lives have been lost because of the dangers created when an individual allegedly chose to flee from law enforcement,” county Prosecutor Peter Lucido said in a press release. The second-degree murder charge carries a penalty of up to life in prison while the other two charges are punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Blackwell is also facing charges from a separate case where he allegedly broke into a Mount Clemens woman’s home on the day before the fatal crash. He is charged with third-degree home invasion and aggravated stalking, both five-year felonies. Blackwell waived his right to a preliminary examination in that case. The double-fatal incident took place March 14 when Blackwell was observed by Clinton Township police speeding southbound on Gratiot Avenue. Officers attempted to stop Blackwell in his 2002 Jeep Cherokee near Quinn Road, but Blackwell allegedly continued to drive at excessive speeds, according to prosecutors. Blackwell’s vehicle was traveling on Gratiot at over 100 mph when it crashed into a Volvo S60 that was headed east on 14 Mile Road, prosecutors said. Assistant Macomb Prosecutor Natalie Sullivan prosecuted the case Thursday.

articles.title: How Michigan's Arab and Muslim voters helped Abdul El-Sayed win a US Senate seat
articles.description: Pre-election polling suggests Michigan Arab and Muslim voters overwhelmingly backed Abdul El-Sayed for Senate. A researcher explains why and details political splits.
articles.content: Tears and embraces fill the room as Abdul El-Sayed celebrates his victory in the Michigan U.S. Senate race on November 4, 2026.(Zena Issa / Michigan Public )A great many constituencies in Michigan came together this week to power Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's victory in the U.S. Senate race over Republican Mike Rogers. The contest especially meant a lot to Arab American and Muslim American voters. It's the first time a lot of Middle Eastern and North African voters might have had a chance to cast a statewide ballot for someone who shared aspects of their cultural background and, in some cases, their perspective on the issues. Nura Sediqe is an assistant professor in the Department of Political Science at Michigan State University, and she’s been looking at some of the key voting blocs that helped propel El-Sayed to a win. April Baer spoke with Sediqe on Stateside.This interview has been edited for length and clarity. April Baer: There was a lot at stake, and a lot of money pouring in, and a lot of eyes locked on this Senate race. What aspects specifically were you keeping an eye on this year? Nura Sediqe: I was really interested in how the anti-Muslim sentiment that was pervasive in some of the campaign ads would impact Michigan voters in the way they see issues. I was also interested in voter turnout and whether we saw how much people prioritized domestic issues of affordability relative to some of the fear. Does fear win or does the economy win was really the frame I was thinking through.AB: A lot of Arab Americans and Muslim Americans have seen language trying to link them, maybe them personally, with terrorism and you know, a lot of very hardcore Islamic ideologies that have nothing to do with their own lives. Is there anything you can tell us about how you've been trying to find out the effect that this had? NS: So at Michigan State, we run a survey called the State of the State Survey with YouGov. And so, we had results come out from early the first two weeks of October. So this is a survey of Michigan voters, likely Michigan voters. And folks were asked if they would vote for a person who was Muslim. And 39% of people in the in the survey said they would not, if the candidate was Muslim, they would not vote for them. And so that's a very compelling statistic. If you think of it point blank, you know, that they're not hiding it. But you're looking at who the who are those 39%? It falls on partisan lines. A lot of them are already voting in the Republican camp and sort of affected by the discourse within that party. But there was still a penalty where coming into the election, what we saw was that Abdul paid a penalty for being Muslim relative to (Governor-elect) Jocelyn Benson, where he was trailing about five points in the pre-election surveys. And, if we controlled for everything else, what stood out was that it was simply his identity background as a Muslim that made him less likely to be voted on coming into the election relative to other Democrats at the top of the ticket.AB: Did you get a sense that there was something in this contest that changed people's minds?NS: I think the youth vote, in terms of the the mobilization early on, the excitement to sort of take an unlikely candidate and mobilize him forward to take on the selection of more established Democratic preferences really played an interesting role. And I think the way that there was cross pressures and concerns around the economy, I think Abdul's campaign … he actually was not the one to bring up identity issues. He was bringing up, you know, money out of politics, you know, like health care. And I think in a lot of ways, that is exactly the pulse of what has hurt everyday citizens in Michigan. Just like you see this wave of folks leaving the Republican Party because of economic concern across the country. So that's not unique to Michigan, but it was definitely felt in Michigan.AB: I know another aspect of elections that you pay attention to is what we can learn of how Arab and Muslim voters have cast ballots. Can you share a little bit about how that's worked out in recent election cycles before this year?NS: I should say that Arab Americans and American Muslims have been a really old community in Michigan, and they're very proud of having deep roots to the state, particularly Southeast Michigan, you know, a lot of auto workers with the auto industry. So you have a very established and old Black Muslim community in Michigan. ... For folks who are unfamiliar with, you know, the history of Black organizing that came from the Black Muslim tradition and is still a sizable, vibrant community in Detroit. And with Arab Americans, we're the only state in the country where we already have a sizable number of folks in local office, a couple mayors who are Arab American. And so you've seen, because they've been here multi generations, an investment in Michigan, in a way. And that shows in their policy preferences where, with the exception of 2024, their key issues of concern have been the same as other Americans polled. Health care, economy, jobs. Those tend to be at the top of their issue priorities in the same way it is for other voters. The only time you saw sort of divergence or sort of like a hiccup was in 2024, when foreign policy and the issue of Palestine sort of entered their voting calculus as an issue of concern.AB: Is it too soon to know how voters who are who are Arab or who are Muslim might have cast their ballots this year?NS: So what we know, we just received the data from likely voters from the University of Chicago's NORC Center where they pulled a sample of folks and they did an oversample of Michigan, and Arab and Muslim voters in Michigan. And so what we found in the pre-election polling is that of the Muslims that were polled, 97% said they were voting for Abdul El-Sayed and 84% for Jocelyn Benson. Interestingly, for Arab voters in Michigan, religion was a divide where Arab Muslims, 98% said they were voting for Abdul, and only 41% of Arab Christians. So Arab Christians are the anomaly. There were the anomaly in 2024. They were the subset that voted for Trump. Arab Muslims did not vote for Trump in 2024. They voted third party in precincts were there heavily Arab, or they voted Democrat Kamala Harris. It was Arab Christians that had voted for Trump. And then coming into this, you saw a split ticket where some did vote for Benson but did not vote for Abdul. But some have remained in the Republican Party. And so there is a larger conversation about the history of this subset of Arab Christian communities in Michigan and why their policy preferences look so different than other Arab Americans in Michigan.

articles.title: US officials unveil $280K deal to help Puerto Rico face water and power crises
articles.source: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has met with nonprofits in Puerto Rico as officials announced a $280,000 partnership to help the U.S. territory confront emergencies SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani met with nonprofits in Puerto Rico on Friday as officials announced a $280,000 partnership to help the U.S. territory confront emergencies. The partnership between Hispanic Federation and the Federal Home Loan Bank of New York comes as Puerto Rico struggles with chronic power outages and intermittent water shortages while it tries to rebuild from Hurricane Maria and other disasters. The nonprofit Hispanic Federation said the money would equip 10 community-run resiliency hubs across the island with increased water storage capacity; some also would receive rain-collection systems, kitchen infrastructure and solar power with battery storage. "Puerto Rico’s families have lived through more disasters than anyone should have to,” said Frankie Miranda, president and CEO of Hispanic Federation. The Federal Home Loan Bank of New York is contributing $210,000 to the effort while Hispanic Federation raised an additional $70,000, officials said. “Conversations about climate change and environmental justice are essential to the wellbeing and future of our communities,” said New York Gov. Kathy Hochul. She and Mamdani are among a group of New York government officials in Puerto Rico for a four-day, annual conference. The announcement comes months after the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump canceled solar projects in Puerto Rico that were supposed to help thousands of low-income families. One project, worth $400 million, would have seen the installation of solar and battery storage systems in low-income homes and those with medical needs. The U.S. Department of Energy has said the money initially slated for solar projects would instead be used to help maintain Puerto Rico’s crumbling power grid, which was razed by Hurricane Maria in September 2017. The grid, however, was already weakened given a lack of maintenance and investment. The decisions prompted outrage on the island as federal support for solar projects fades. Last week, six Puerto Rico residents sued the U.S. Energy Department and its secretary, Chris Wright, following the scrapping of a $1 billion federally funded program to provide solar power and battery storage to those who most needed it. “The cost of such systems remains out of reach for the majority of Puerto Ricans,” the lawsuit stated. Among those suing is 63-year-old Arecibo resident Ileana Ríos, who is diabetic and needs to refrigerate her insulin. Meanwhile, her son has asthma and needs to use a nebulizer, which requires electricity. The lawsuit noted that Ríos “regularly loses power when the weather is stable and always loses power during storms, sometimes for several weeks at a time.” The other residents who sued also have serious health conditions and need equipment or medications that rely on electricity. The lawsuit requests that a judge order the U.S. Energy Department to reinstate the grant program, among other things. The U.S. Department of Energy did not immediately return a message seeking comment. The funding loss has been a blow to nonprofits and others who faced months of uncertainty and confusion as they awaited the Trump administration’s decision on whether and how it would continue the program. “We had a lot of uncertainty. ... At some points it just felt like we were talking to no one," said Sybelle Rodriguez del Valle, director of operations at the energy resilience nonprofit Barrio Eléctrico, which was part of the U.S. Energy Department program. Barrio Eléctrico provides electric service to more than 500 families across 12 municipalities in Puerto Rico and was poised to provide resilient energy for 1,200 families with funds from the federal program. It had only completed about one-third of its projects before the program ended, losing an estimated $16 million to $20 million in funding. Associated Press reporter Gabriela Aoun Angueira contributed to this report. 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

articles.description: Next week, experts will determine if the US has lost its measles elimination status.
articles.content: An infant in Wisconsin has died of measles, the first measles death in the state since 1990, officials reported Thursday. The death comes amid an outbreak in the Badger State that has stricken over 430 people across 13 counties this year. "Any death of a child is a tragedy, and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Wisconsin Health Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family." The baby's death is the third measles fatality nationally just this week, following the death of a New York child reported on Monday and another death in Pennsylvania reported on Wednesday. The Pennsylvania death was of an unvaccinated person in Jefferson County; the state health department did not provide additional details, such as the age of the person. articles.title: For Spartans and Wolverines, annual rivalry game takes on different stakes this year
articles.description: Michigan and Michigan State will play their annual rivalry football game on Saturday. Michigan Public's John U. Bacon discusses that, plus the Detroit Lions' next matchup.
articles.content: Michigan State coach Pat Fitzgerald (left) and Michigan coach Kyle Whittingham are both making their debuts in the annual rivalry game between the Spartans and Wolverines. They’ll play Saturday evening in Ann Arbor.(Mark J. Terrill (left) and Al Goldis (right) / AP Photo)Michigan and Michigan State will meet this weekend in Ann Arbor for their annual football rivalry game. How do the stakes shift when both teams have had their struggles? For more on that and the Detroit Lions' quest to extend their winning streak, Michigan Public sports commentator John U. Bacon joined Morning Edition host Doug Tribou. DT: In college football, Michigan got a conference win over Rutgers last weekend behind a stronger performance by freshman quarterback Tommy Carr. But the Wolverines are 5-3, not where they had hoped to be at this point in the season. Michigan State, however, is in worse shape. The Spartans have lost six straight and are 0-5 against Big Ten teams. On Saturday, these two teams will meet on the field. You touched on this last week, John, but how do down years — especially when both teams are somewhat down — affect rivalry games and vice versa?JUB: Henry Kissinger himself. How about [his] quote on this?DT: That's where I was expecting we'd start. [Laughs] JUB: Of course, it's the obvious one. His great line about academics is: the academic fights at Harvard are so fierce because the stakes are so low. Here we are, Doug. I think this is going to be a more intense game, because neither team is playing for anything else at this point. And to lose this game for Michigan, of course, means you're going to hear about it for a whole year.DT: And Michigan's rivalry with Ohio State gets the most attention. But what do you like about the energy and the long history between MSU and U of M?JUB: Well, it's an underrated rivalry. It should be a nationally acclaimed rivalry in my opinion. A lot of great back and forth, a lot of great Michigan State teams. It's rare for both teams to be riding high at the same time. The big difference between the Michigan-Ohio State rivalry is you will never see a Buckeye at a Wolverine tailgate, or vice versa. When you walk around Ann Arbor on Saturday, you will see almost all the tailgates are what I would call "integrated" with [Michigan State] green and [Michigan] blue, which I think is very refreshing. And the last 58 contests... okay, Michigan has won 40, but of the 18 Michigan State victories, 11 were upsets. Nobody is better at upsetting the Wolverines — by a long shot — than the Spartans. So, Michigan fans, heads up.DT: Who do you like to win the Paul Bunyan Trophy this year?JUB: Who's more likely to lose it in this case? [Laughs] Michigan's not a very good team, and Michigan State is worse. And then they got injured. So I have to go with Michigan. But again, this is the classic "throw out the records" game.DT: The Lions got a major win over the previously undefeated Minnesota Vikings last weekend. But that outcome was tempered by a serious neck injury to linebacker Jack Campbell after making a tackle. Campbell was motionless, face down on the field. On Wednesday, though, he released a statement saying he had full movement in his lower body, but still has work to do to regain movement in his upper body. Obviously, some good news there, John, but the whole story is a reminder of how violent the game of football is that so many of us watch.JUB: Well, exactly right. And the NFL and football in general has done a very good job of changing the protocols, the procedures to reduce the number of traumatic injuries, including concussions, in the game. And the progress there is tremendous, but it's still a violent game. And that's why many still perceive that watching the game is a guilty pleasure. And this is more proof that there's a lot of risk.DT: Well, with Campbell on their minds, the Lions will be back on the field on Sunday to face the Dolphins in Miami. The Dolphins have struggled this season. They're just 1-6. They have not been scoring a lot of points, but have also managed to give up quite a few, and that's usually not the greatest combination. [Laugh] I assume this game for the Lions falls into your category of "win the games you're supposed to win."JUB: I think this is the whole category, in this case. The Dolphins represent that. You mentioned earlier they're struggling. Doug, the Dolphins are aspiring to struggle. That's kind of the reach goal for them on Sunday.DT: [Laughs] That's the new bumper sticker for my car.JUB: [Laughs] Leave me alone. I'm aspiring to struggle.DT: [Laughs] That's right. Also, back off.JUB: I think at that point they're going to, Doug.DT: [Laughs] John, thanks a lot. Have a good weekend.JUB: Thank you.Editor's note: Some quotes in this article have been lightly edited for length and clarity. You can play the full audio of the interview near the top of this page.The University of Michigan holds Michigan Public's broadcast license.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan propels ‘Medicare for All’ debate
articles.description: Progressive victories in the midterm elections have reignited calls for 'Medicare for All' as voters struggle with rising healthcare costs, but critics warn of ‘huge' political risks.
articles.content: LANSING — Fifteen years working as an emergency room nurse has convinced Kim Bogan that the only way to fix the American healthcare system is to tear it down and start over. Her patients arriving for triage are sicker than ever. They can’t afford many of the prescriptions they get in the ER. And sometimes when patients die, she wonders if she could have saved them had she not been caring for five or six other people at once. That’s why she spent the past year shuttling between 12-hour shifts at this city’s Sparrow Hospital and campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat who made “Medicare for All” a signature issue in his congressional campaign and is now a senator-elect. But she realizes that just because progressive candidates successfully campaigned on some form of the policy in states such as Texas, Iowa, Maine, and Michigan, it doesn’t mean Medicare for All will be an easy sell. “Nobody expected that,” Bogan said. Medicare for All typically refers to a government health program that would guarantee Americans coverage by replacing most or all private insurance. Critics are already pointing out that, even in a blue wave as massive as the 2026 midterms, the most vocal Medicare for All champions generally won by smaller margins than more moderate Democrats. Related: ‘A beautifully American story’: El-Sayed’s win resonates with Muslim Americans How Abdul El-Sayed, Jocelyn Benson won Michigan: Big turnout, Democratic shifts Bridge Listens Issues Watch recap: Behind the Democrat rout in Michigan “Whatever else people voted for in this midterm election — anger about inflation, anger about corruption, anger about the Iran war — they by and large didn’t vote to have the government take over health insurance,” said Jonathan Oberlander, a professor and healthcare reform expert at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill. Still, supporters of universal healthcare see this moment as a once-in-a-generation opportunity because Americans are buckling under the weight of healthcare costs and are hungry for change. Several states, including Oregon, are already exploring what it would take to set up single-payer systems. The affordability crisis “dominated this election, and Medicare for All speaks to that,” Oberlander said. Medicare for All supporters expect the policy agenda will gain major momentum heading into the 2028 Democratic presidential primaries, he said. But more moderate Democrats may see the idea’s growing popularity as a threat to gains they made in states such as Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina. “If Democrats want to hold those seats, which were very difficult to win, they’re probably not interested in passing Medicare for All,” Oberlander said. “That’s a huge political risk in red-leaning states. So just because Democrats have a majority doesn’t mean it’s a majority for Medicare for All.”Donate Previous Medicare for All proposals would have required getting millions of people to willingly give up their existing coverage, fueling unprecedented opposition from the healthcare industry, said Michael Cannon, a healthcare economist at the libertarian Cato Institute and a Medicare for All opponent. “If Medicare for All actually had the price levels that Bernie Sanders and Abdul El-Sayed envision, the industry would tear it to shreds,” he said. And even as voters say they support Medicare for All in greater numbers than in nearly a decade, support falters when they’re presented with common arguments against it — like it could lead to higher taxes or delays in treatment — according to a recent KFF poll. Jaime Bardenhagen said she feels a little guilty about the idea of getting her healthcare coverage from the government. A former nurse in rural Leelanau County in northern Michigan, Bardenhagen has Parkinson’s and sialidosis, a rare genetic disease that can cause seizures. Yet she “feels bad” about qualifying for disability benefits next year. Such programs were something she “didn’t believe in” while growing up on a farm, she said. You were supposed to work for what you needed, she said, not rely on government support. “And I did work as hard as I could, for as long as I could.” But like millions of Americans, Bardenhagen and her husband saw their health insurance costs skyrocket this year, after enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies expired. Their monthly premiums went from $700 to $1,300, with a deductible of $7,500. They started putting off medical tests her doctor wanted, she said. “We couldn’t afford that,” she said. Her husband voted for Donald Trump in 2016, Bardenhagen said. This time, he stayed home. Bardenhagen, a Democrat, also considered sitting out the midterms. “I just don’t trust either party anymore,” she said. Despite those misgivings, she says she supports Medicare for All. Her years as a nurse left her disillusioned with the current healthcare system, she said. She felt the insurance companies, not doctors, were calling the shots, determining which prescriptions and procedures patients could receive. Wouldn’t it be fairer, she figured, if “good people” in government were making those calls? “So, absolutely, the government should take it over.” That takeover is Cannon’s worst-case scenario. The libertarian economist said giving the federal government greater control over the healthcare system would only backfire. Patients would be left “in even more vulnerable positions, because they would be relying for their access to healthcare on government spending that is just not sustainable.” Medicare for All supporters are naive to think the government could negotiate lower drug and healthcare prices by replacing private plans with a public one, he said. “Everyone knows that the industry is going to end up running the show, and that has been the case since they passed Medicare,” Cannon said. For Bardenhagen, the message she wants Democrats to take from the midterms is simple: “Do something,” the former nurse said. “With the election results, both parties are going to be under pressure to come up with solutions to address the current affordability crisis in healthcare,” said Sara Collins, a senior scholar at the Commonwealth Fund, a private foundation that supports healthcare research. That could mean smaller, but still significant, bipartisan deals that might have seemed unthinkable before the midterms: things such as reinstating the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired at the end of last year, or other measures with broad support, such as curbing insurance companies’ use of prior authorizations, which requires patients to get insurers’ approval before proceeding with a covered treatment. “That’s probably the lowest-hanging fruit for them, I’d think,” said Patricia Votava, a political strategist based in Sullivan’s Island, South Carolina. The pressure for healthcare reform is likely to grow, too, with Affordable Care Act premiums set to rise by double digits again next year; employers passing on more of their growing insurance premium costs to workers; and massive cuts to Medicaid looming, which are projected to leave 7.5 million more people uninsured by 2034. On the whole, the midterm results could push Democrats’ healthcare agenda further left, Oberlander said. Some Democrats could support a public option, a government-backed health plan people could opt into. Others in the party could coalesce around a version of Medicare for All that doesn’t fully replace private insurance but serves as “guaranteed baseline government health insurance,” as El-Sayed described his current plan in the campaign. “If you like your insurance from your employer or from your union, that can still be there for you,” he said. Whatever they opt for, Democrats shouldn’t expect voters to be willing to wait patiently for years of gradual change, Oberlander said. “If the window opens, you better jump right through.” South Carolina correspondent Lauren Sausser contributed to this report. articles.title: Urine or not? A different kind of MSU-U of M rivals contest
articles.description: You know those Calvin stickers on the backs of cars? A cartoon kid peeing on random things, like a team you hate? Real-ass wastewater scientists from the two universities are […]
articles.content: You know those Calvin stickers on the backs of cars? A cartoon kid peeing on random things, like a team you hate? Real-ass wastewater scientists from the two universities are asking people to join a “Piss Off” at the Big House in Ann Arbor to determine which team is more full of piss and get some science out of the deal too. There will be yurts – this is not a permission slip to pee willy-nilly around A2 – for taking care of number one at the Ann Arbor Golf & Outing Course, with volunteers (we have questions) who will direct fans, along with anyone else who is interested in peeing for bragging rights. Collections will only be allowed, at this time, from people who stand up to pee, according to a release from the Department of Sociology and the College of Social Science. Collections begin at noon and will continue until 8 p.m., so drink up. A processed urine-based fertilizer is applied to the Matthaei Botanical Gardens. Courtesy of University of Michigan The urine will be collected and turned into a nutrient-rich fertilizer for horticultural crops, a process called “peecycling,” according to the release, authored by Karessa Weir. https://sociology.msu.edu/news/pissoff11426.html The event is being funded in part by a University Research Council Grant awarded to Gasteyer and Sociology Assistant Professor Saleh Ahmed. Also working on the project is Sociology PhD student Autumn Bland. “There are two reasons for the event,” Gasteyer said, according to Weir. “One is to actually collect the urine which can be used to produce the fertilizer but the other is to educate people that what comes out of our bodies naturally provides nutrients that can help things grow. “The way we currently treat urine involves a lot of energy and resources and we end up disposing of those nutrients when the entire process could be much more beneficial to the whole world.” U.S. regulations restrict the use of urine on food crops but it can be used widely on horticultural crops such as grass lawns and flower fields both commercially and personally, Gasteyer said. “It will provide you with truly beautiful peonies in the front of your house,” he said. The urine-to-fertilizer production is the life’s work of Dr. Nancy Love, civil and environmental engineer at University of Michigan. Her lab needs the raw product to better scale up the process of converting urine to fertilizer and make it available for household uses. It is modeled off Vermont’s Rich Earth Institute’s annual “Piss Off” competition, which is also collaborating on this project. “Our department is home to the nation’s first university-based end-to-end peecycling demo system. And that includes a new toilet designed to separate out urine for both seated and standing users which is targeted to hit the market later this year,” Love said. The finished product will be used in both UM and MSU agricultural fields including at MSU’s Kellogg Biological Center and UM’s Matthaei Botanical Gardens. For full details on how the Piss Off works, please go to this link: https://pissoff.engin.umich.edu/

‘I didn’t expect to be a main character’: Abdul El-Sayed heads to the Senate with a mandate – and a spotlight
articles.content: The successful Democratic contender for a Michigan Senate seat parried the many insinuations lobbed by Republicans What happens after the ‘blue wave’? Ask your midterm election results questions Abdul El-Sayed said he did not expect to be “a main character of this midterms”, but the first Muslim elected to the US Senate in history will take his seat in January after a vitriolic campaign that cast him as the central villain of the president and his party. By October he told the Associated Press he was “not shying away” from those rightwing fixations. “What are you implying?” El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, replied when a town hall attender asked if he would disavow the Muslim Brotherhood, in a now-viral exchange. On Tuesday, Michigan voters helped the pugnacious progressive cap off a transcendental blue wave nationwide, defeating his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, by about seven points, 52.5% to 45.5%. “My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed,” he said at the beginning of his victory speech in downtown Detroit on Tuesday night, as the crowd erupted in cheers. He then thanked the voters of Michigan, for taking a “chance on the unlikeliest of candidates”. He won with majorities among Black voters and Jewish early voters, and with a larger share of the vote than Kamala Harris or senator Elissa Slotkin in 2024 in Wayne, Oakland and Macomb counties, despite Republican attacks on his faith and objections from some Jewish leaders to his stance on Israel. Now he takes that mandate to Washington as one of the most visible Democrats to have emerged from this election cycle. “He is a charismatic, social media-savvy politician, so he will come to DC with a lot more initial interest than most freshman politicians,” said Matt Grossmann, director of Michigan State University’s Institute for Public Policy and Social Research. “He won’t be able to say he had some sort of unique vision that worked above all others, but he will be able to say people said he couldn’t win in a swing state, and he did. I think that will matter.” The test, according to Shekar Narasimhan, founder and chair of the AAPI Victory Fund, a Super Pac focused on Asian American and Pacific Islander political power, is less about identity than delivery. “I think the onus on Abdul is less about being the first Muslim senator. Obviously, there is a weight for that, but it’s more about how he represents Michigan given the $165m that was thrown at him in both the primary and the general election,” Narasimhan said. “I think he does have to carry an agenda, and I think the caucus is going to give him some leadership position to be able to carry it out.” For many Arab and Muslim Americans, the result was vindication. Maya Berry, executive director of the Arab American Institute, called voters’ rejection of the attacks on El-Sayed “tremendous” for “every little boy named Abdul, every little girl named Zainab”, arguing that the question at stake was whether the country supports an inclusive democracy. Donald Trump and other Republicans repeatedly used Islamophobia to target his faith. At a rally in Port Huron on 25 October, the president baselessly called El-Sayed a jihadist and a Muslim Brotherhood member, said he was “on the side of the terrorists”, and claimed he would “have to go through a metal detector” before entering the Senate. John Kennedy, the senator from Louisiana, said El-Sayed “sleeps in a Bin Laden jersey”, while Ted Cruz, the senator from Texas, called him a “jihadist leprechaun”, and JD Vance called him “evil”. Campaign mailers paid for by the Senate Leadership Fund, a prominent Republican Super Pac, and seen by the Guardian would link El-Sayed with Sharia law, with text that said his specific views “dictates how women dress”, “requires women have a guardian” and “prohibits women from divorcing”. El-Sayed dismissed those attacks, quipping that he supported “shawarma law”. On election night, Dearborn’s mayor, Abdullah Hammoud, said voters chose El-Sayed “regardless of the direction in which he prays”. He called it “a beautifully American story”. Get the most important news as it breaks Some Jewish leaders, such as the Detroit community director for the American Jewish Committee, Amy Sapeika, said El-Sayed’s rhetoric, and even his victory speech, made many in the community “feel excluded as Jews and as people who support Israel”. While exit polls and preliminary analyses show that a majority of Michigan Jews voted for El-Sayed, his margins in heavily Jewish communities trailed other Democrats in the state, such as the governor-elect, Jocelyn Benson. In West Bloomfield, where a synagogue attack took place in March, Rogers’s share of the vote rose to 46% from 42% two years ago, when he ran against Slotkin for the Senate. El-Sayed would reach the same parity with Black voters as Slotkin’s win in 2024, where he won about 86% compared to her 85%, according to an exit poll by NBC. On Israel, El-Sayed has not changed his position since being elected. On election day morning, Trump said on Fox & Friends that roughly $4bn in annual US military aid to Israel would be “cut off at the end of the year”, citing “lunatics like an El-Sayed”. El-Sayed, who campaigned on ending the aid, welcomed the announcement and called for an end to arms sales as well. While Congress appropriates the aid, Grossmann said Trump had “basically credited Abdul with changing his position on aid to Israel”, giving him an early win. Narasimhan called the announcement “a good starting point”. He said efforts by Bernie Sanders and other Democrats to restrict offensive weapons were “as far as he’s going to get in this environment on Israel”. Asked on CNN on Thursday about working with the president and vice-president, El-Sayed made clear he was not softening his tone. He said he would “take every opportunity” to “differentiate between what JD Vance says and what JD Vance does”, and that he finds the pair “odious” in how they behave outside their official roles. But he also said he would work with them. “I’ll work with anybody to serve the people of the state of Michigan,” he said. “If they’re serious about doing that, let’s get some stuff done.”

articles.title: UN climate talks start in the year of disasters, energy price shocks and fast rising temperatures
articles.description: UN climate talks start in the year of disasters, energy price shocks and fast rising temperatures AP News COP31 and Climate Action’s New Centers of Gravity Council on Foreign Relations UN climate talks start in a year of disasters, energy price shocks and fast rising temperatures NBC News Global Science Panel Hits Roadblocks Ahead of COP31 Climate Summit Inside Climate News Cop31 will expose the conflicts and contrad
articles.content: Three stories about climate change are playing out like popular movie genres as United Nations climate negotiations begin in Antalya, Turkey. There’s the horror story. Many scientists believe global warming is accelerating. Two months ago, the U.N. readjusted its decade-old goal of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) because the world is blowing past that threshold. The fallout from rising temperatures is felt globally, with Europe’s deadly summer heat waves and Nepal’s devastating flooding as stark examples. There’s the love triangle. For more than a century, the world has been powered by coal, oil and gas. This love affair spurred economic development, as well as the emissions warming the planet. But renewable energy is capturing some of the world’s attention because it’s cheaper and cleaner than fossil fuels. Instead of switching from one to the other, the world is using both to meet demand from power-hungry artificial intelligence and ever-growing economic development. This isn’t helping curb climate change. Then there’s the war movie. Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine triggered a European energy shock. This year the United States and Israel bombed Iran. The conflict closed the Strait of Hormuz and sent fossil fuel prices skyrocketing, forcing nations to rethink their energy systems. These stories are colliding as the 31st Conference of Parties, or COP31, starts Monday with speeches from world leaders and will later dig into how to follow through on past climate pledges. A person cools off at a cooling mist spot on a hot and sunny day at the Sensoji Buddhist temple in Tokyo’s Asakusa district on Aug. 7, 2026. (AP Photo/Eugene Hoshiko, File) A person cools off at a cooling mist spot on a hot and sunny day at the Sensoji Buddhist temple in Tokyo’s Asakusa district on Aug. 7, 2026. (AP Photo/Eugene Hoshiko, File) A key issue this year is the implementation of promises to transition away from fossil fuels. Co-host Turkey is also pushing a separate plan that would help do that by shifting more global energy use — including transportation — to electricity generated from solar and wind power. Negotiators also will hash out how to provide promised funds to poor countries to switch to renewables, adapt to a warmer world and recover from climate-induced damage. “It’s really the moment that we place a magnifying lens on what’s happening in the world on climate change, both good and bad,” David Waskow, international climate chief at the World Resources Institute, said. While the U.S. is the world’s largest historic carbon polluter, it skipped last year’s COP and isn’t expected to participate this year. “There’s always two topics in the climate negotiations that are relevant and difficult,” said Niklas Höhne, co-founder of Germany’s NewClimate Institute. “The first one is who produces emissions (and) how much. That is difficult enough. But what is even more complicated is the other issue, and that is who pays. And on this one, we are particularly in a difficult situation because the U.S., as the largest contributor, has dropped out. And there’s no other player who can jump in.” Wildfires spread near the municipality of Iranduba, Amazonas state, Brazil, Oct. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/Edmar Barros, File) Wildfires spread near the municipality of Iranduba, Amazonas state, Brazil, Oct. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/Edmar Barros, File) Eleven years ago, the world was on track to hit 4 C (7.2 F) of warming above preindustrial levels by the end of the century. In 2015, nations set the goal of keeping warming to below 2 C (3.6 F), but with a preferred limit of 1.5 C (2.7 F), as measured over a multi-year period. Now, the world is at 1.4 C (2.5 F) of warming and is hurtling toward 2.6 C (4.7 F), the U.N. found. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to end up as the second year to exceed the 1.5 degree Celsius level, behind 2024, the European climate agency Copernicus announced Friday. “We have failed so far,” said Johan Rockström, director of Germany’s Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. Rockström said Earth will likely experience more extreme weather, such as floods, droughts and storms, and may soon reach “tipping points,” such as ocean currents changing and the Amazon rainforest collapsing. A man rides past an operating oil pumpjack in Cabimas, Venezuela, Aug. 31, 2026. (AP Photo/Ariana Cubillos, File) A man rides past an operating oil pumpjack in Cabimas, Venezuela, Aug. 31, 2026. (AP Photo/Ariana Cubillos, File) Even though burning fossil fuels is the main cause of warming, it has rarely been targeted in final documents agreed upon at the conference, mostly because those decisions require consensus. “The reason we are seeing the breach of 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming is because we avoided the absolutely fundamental question of how climate change happened and what’s responsible, the source of the problem and that’s fossil fuels,” said Harjeet Singh, founding director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. “Unless and until we resolve the issue of fossil fuel phase out, we will not be able to deal with the problem.” Brazil, which hosted COP30 last year, this month released a detailed voluntary roadmap for how countries could transition away from fossil fuels. The roadmap is meant to turn the “big problem” of reducing fossil fuels into “smaller actionable solutions,” Ana Toni, who served as CEO of last year’s climate talks, said. One key thing nations must do is stop subsidizing fossil fuels, she said. The U.N. estimates fossil fuel subsidies globally hit $1.1 trillion this year. “What’s standing in the way is not so much technology as governments and incumbent industries,” said Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics. “One cannot underestimate the power and influence of the fossil fuel industry in slowing down action.” Activists hang banners while participating in a demonstration at the COP30 U.N. Climate Summit, Nov. 21, 2025, in Belem, Brazil. (AP Photo/Andre Penner, File) Activists hang banners while participating in a demonstration at the COP30 U.N. Climate Summit, Nov. 21, 2025, in Belem, Brazil. (AP Photo/Andre Penner, File) Barbados youth activist Ashley Lashley’s first COP was five years ago. She was frustrated by the lack of progress then, but hopeful because there was urgency to keep the 1.5-degree goal alive. Lashley still attends negotiations with some hope, but she is more frustrated than ever. She said “the science has become more alarming, but yet politically we seem to be negotiating how much failure we are prepared to tolerate.” Qiyun Woo, a Singaporean youth environmentalist, said her generation is tired of “seeing their present and futures blanketed in wildfire smoke, in devastating floods (and) landslides.” What gives most experts hope is how cheap solar and wind energy are, along with electric car growth, strengthening the economic argument for transitioning away from fossil fuels. “It has never been as easy to reduce emissions as it is today because, again, this year, renewable energy has been developing faster than before,” Höhne said. Wind turbines generate electricity in Balabanli, near Tekirdag, northwestern Turkey, Oct. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/Emrah Gurel, File) Wind turbines generate electricity in Balabanli, near Tekirdag, northwestern Turkey, Oct. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/Emrah Gurel, File) Much of the work at climate negotiations happens on the sidelines, where not everyone has to agree and some nations do more than others. One important sideline initiative this year is Turkey’s goal of increasing electricity’s share of global energy use from 21% to 35% by 2035, preferably by using renewable power. Mohamed Adow, a veteran COP observer and director of Power Shift Africa, said the conference is taking place at a time when the world is deeply fragmented. “The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has intensified economic and energy security pressures,” he said. “We don’t expect this particular conference to be able to sufficiently respond to the present day challenge ... that is affecting livelihoods and economies.” The climate talks are hindered by the continued absence of the U.S., Adow said, adding that it wasn’t fair to nations like Nepal, which have to face catastrophic destruction alone while the world’s wealthiest country and biggest polluter sits on the fence. “A time will come when we will have to hold the U.S. accountable for the climate harms that it’s caused,” he said. Borenstein reported from Washington, Delgado from Bangkok and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.
