articles.title: DTE, Consumers sue to block ‘money out of politics’ proposal approved by voters
articles.description: Michigan’s biggest utility companies are suing to block implementation of Proposal 2, arguing voter-approved restrictions on political giving violate free speech rights.
articles.content: Michigan utilities sue over Proposal 2, which passed Tuesday with more than 80% of the vote Law bans utilities and some state contractors from donating to political campaigns, among other things Lawsuit alleges that violates free speech and other constitutional rights LANSING — Two days after Michigan voters overwhelmingly approved Proposal 2, DTE Energy and Consumers Energy on Thursday sued to stop implementation of new restrictions on their political giving. This story also appeared in Bridge Michigan The state’s largest utilities argue that the new law — approved by more than 80% of voters in Tuesday’s election — will violate their free speech rights and other provisions of the US Constitution. Proposal 2 aims to prohibit direct or indirect contributions to Michigan politicians by the utilities or companies with more than $250,000 in state government contracts, along with immediate family members and other people with close connections. But in a complaint filed with the US District Court for the Western District of Michigan, the utilities argued the proposal violates free speech and association rights guaranteed by the First Amendment and the Fourteenth Amendment’s due process clause. Absent an injunction, the companies “will be forced to choose between surrendering their rights to political association and risking substantial penalties for exercising them,” attorneys wrote. Policymakers and voters benefit from hearing Consumers’ perspective on debates over reliability, affordability and clean energy “even if they may sometimes disagree with it,” they added. Related: Michigan elections: Voters approve Proposal 2 Money Out of Politics question Michigan midterm voters cite costs, government spending, culture wars and Trump Now, the hard part: Jocelyn Benson has big plans. Michigan has big problems The suit seeks a court order barring enforcement by the state. It names Michigan Bureau of Elections Director Jonathan Brater, Attorney General Dana Nessel and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (now the governor-elect) as defendants. The lawsuit is “no surprise,” said Maura Cowley, manager of the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics campaign, which argues the law will “end pay-to-play politics” in Lansing. “The corporations bankrolling our opposition have been gearing up for this lawsuit since Proposal 2 first qualified for the ballot, if not before,” Cowley said in a statement. The group is “confident Proposal 2 will withstand legal scrutiny, and we were fully expecting and are prepared to take on this and any legal challenge,” she added. It’s already the second lawsuit over Proposal 2. The Mackinac Center for Public Policy announced a legal challenge Tuesday night after it became clear voters had approved the measure. While opposition groups had argued the proposal would violate free speech rights, the utility lawsuit argues the new law also violates the Fourteenth Amendment because it is too vague in its reasons as to why utilities shouldn’t be able to continue donating to candidates — as well as who the proposal applies to working at or with these companies. The complaint also contends the law violates the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause by “impermissibly” targeting utilities “and a broad swath of people associated with utilities.” The US Supreme Court has generally held that political spending by corporations is protected speech, most notably in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, but courts have looked more favorably on narrowly tailored proposals aimed at limiting corruption. The law “unfairly targets a Michigan business,” along with its employees and their families, Consumers Energy spokesperson Katie Carey said in a statement. “Michiganders should not lose their First Amendment rights because of where they work.” Corporations are already barred from directly giving to candidates in Michigan. The proposal would extend that ban to an affected company’s president, CEO, treasurer, similar officials, board members, people with “substantial” ownership — and their family members. One of the plaintiffs in the suit is the 86-year-old mother of DTE’s treasurer, who would be barred from donating to political candidates “even though she has no role at any utility,” according to the suit. The proposal would restrict political contributions to: The governor, attorney general, state senator, representative or candidate for such office A state or local party committee A committee, other than an independent expenditure committee or ballot question committee, that makes contributions to a candidate A member of the Michigan Public Service Commission Company officials and immediate family members could also not donate to entities that are affiliated with elected officials or candidates and pay for their travel, meals, conference fees or other expenses. Consumers and DTE have spent on political races through employee-funded PACs and “dark money” nonprofits that don’t have to disclose donors. The proposal would require disclosure by groups that reference candidates or ballot issues in so-called issue ads. The proposal would not prohibit contributions to independent expenditure super PACs allowed under Citizens United, but it includes language that had anticipated potential legal challenges: “If any portion is found void, invalid or unenforceable, the remaining portions remain in effect.” This article first appeared on Bridge Michigan and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.

Midterm wave sets a course for ‘Medicare for All’ fight
articles.description: Rising healthcare costs and midterm gains give Medicare for All new momentum, though progressive Democrats face resistance to single-payer reform.
articles.content: Kim Bogan, an emergency room nurse in Michigan, spent the past year campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed, because she believes “Medicare for All” is the best way to fix a broken healthcare system. The patients she sees coming into the ER have often put off getting care, even as their conditions deteriorated. (Kate Wells / KFF Health News)LANSING — Fifteen years working as an emergency room nurse has convinced Kim Bogan that the only way to fix the American healthcare system is to tear it down and start over.Her patients arriving for triage are sicker than ever. They can’t afford many of the prescriptions they get in the ER. And sometimes when patients die, she wonders if she could have saved them had she not been caring for five or six other people at once.That’s why she spent the past year shuttling between 12-hour shifts at this city’s Sparrow Hospital and campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat who made “Medicare for All” a signature issue in his congressional campaign and is now a senator-elect.But she realizes that just because progressive candidates successfully campaigned on some form of the policy in states such as Texas, Iowa, Maine, and Michigan, it doesn’t mean Medicare for All will be an easy sell. “Nobody expected that,” Bogan said.Medicare for All typically refers to a government health program that would guarantee Americans coverage by replacing most or all private insurance. Critics are already pointing out that, even in a blue wave as massive as the 2026 midterms, the most vocal Medicare for All champions generally won by smaller margins than more moderate Democrats.“Whatever else people voted for in this midterm election — anger about inflation, anger about corruption, anger about the Iran war — they by and large didn’t vote to have the government take over health insurance,” said Jonathan Oberlander, a professor and healthcare reform expert at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill.Still, supporters of universal healthcare see this moment as a once-in-a-generation opportunity because Americans are buckling under the weight of healthcare costs and are hungry for change. Several states, including Oregon, are already exploring what it would take to set up single-payer systems.The affordability crisis “dominated this election, and Medicare for All speaks to that,” Oberlander said. Medicare for All supporters expect the policy agenda will gain major momentum heading into the 2028 Democratic presidential primaries, he said.But more moderate Democrats may see the idea’s growing popularity as a threat to gains they made in states such as Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina. “If Democrats want to hold those seats, which were very difficult to win, they’re probably not interested in passing Medicare for All,” Oberlander said. “That’s a huge political risk in red-leaning states. So just because Democrats have a majority doesn’t mean it’s a majority for Medicare for All.”Previous Medicare for All proposals would have required getting millions of people to willingly give up their existing coverage, fueling unprecedented opposition from the healthcare industry, said Michael Cannon, a healthcare economist at the libertarian Cato Institute and a Medicare for All opponent.“If Medicare for All actually had the price levels that Bernie Sanders and Abdul El-Sayed envision, the industry would tear it to shreds,” he said.And even as voters say they support Medicare for All in greater numbers than in nearly a decade, support falters when they’re presented with common arguments against it — like it could lead to higher taxes or delays in treatment — according to a recent KFF poll.Jaime Bardenhagen said she feels a little guilty about the idea of getting her healthcare coverage from the government. A former nurse in rural Leelanau County in northern Michigan, Bardenhagen has Parkinson’s and sialidosis, a rare genetic disease that can cause seizures.Yet she “feels bad” about qualifying for disability benefits next year. Such programs were something she “didn’t believe in” while growing up on a farm, she said. You were supposed to work for what you needed, she said, not rely on government support. “And I did work as hard as I could, for as long as I could.”But like millions of Americans, Bardenhagen and her husband saw their health insurance costs skyrocket this year, after enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies expired.Their monthly premiums went from $700 to $1,300, with a deductible of $7,500. They started putting off medical tests her doctor wanted, she said. “We couldn’t afford that,” she said.Her husband voted for Donald Trump in 2016, Bardenhagen said. This time, he stayed home. Bardenhagen, a Democrat, also considered sitting out the midterms. “I just don’t trust either party anymore,” she said.Despite those misgivings, she says she supports Medicare for All. Her years as a nurse left her disillusioned with the current healthcare system, she said.She felt the insurance companies, not doctors, were calling the shots, determining which prescriptions and procedures patients could receive. Wouldn’t it be fairer, she figured, if “good people” in government were making those calls? “So, absolutely, the government should take it over.”That takeover is Cannon’s worst-case scenario. The libertarian economist said giving the federal government greater control over the healthcare system would only backfire. Patients would be left “in even more vulnerable positions, because they would be relying for their access to healthcare on government spending that is just not sustainable.”Medicare for All supporters are naive to think the government could negotiate lower drug and healthcare prices by replacing private plans with a public one, he said. “Everyone knows that the industry is going to end up running the show, and that has been the case since they passed Medicare,” Cannon said.For Bardenhagen, the message she wants Democrats to take from the midterms is simple: “Do something,” the former nurse said.“With the election results, both parties are going to be under pressure to come up with solutions to address the current affordability crisis in healthcare,” said Sara Collins, a senior scholar at the Commonwealth Fund, a private foundation that supports healthcare research.That could mean smaller, but still significant, bipartisan deals that might have seemed unthinkable before the midterms: things such as reinstating the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired at the end of last year, or other measures with broad support, such as curbing insurance companies’ use of prior authorizations, which requires patients to get insurers’ approval before proceeding with a covered treatment.“That’s probably the lowest-hanging fruit for them, I’d think,” said Patricia Votava, a political strategist based in Sullivan’s Island, South Carolina.The pressure for healthcare reform is likely to grow, too, with Affordable Care Act premiums set to rise by double digits again next year; employers passing on more of their growing insurance premium costs to workers; and massive cuts to Medicaid looming, which are projected to leave 7.5 million more people uninsured by 2034.On the whole, the midterm results could push Democrats’ healthcare agenda further left, Oberlander said. Some Democrats could support a public option, a government-backed health plan people could opt into. Others in the party could coalesce around a version of Medicare for All that doesn’t fully replace private insurance but serves as “guaranteed baseline government health insurance,” as El-Sayed described his current plan in the campaign.“If you like your insurance from your employer or from your union, that can still be there for you,” he said.Whatever they opt for, Democrats shouldn’t expect voters to be willing to wait patiently for years of gradual change, Oberlander said. “If the window opens, you better jump right through.”

articles.title: No more Cybertrucks; Musk moves on from the angular metallic flop
articles.description: Tesla wanted to unseat the Ford F-150, instead it made the Edsel look successful.
articles.content: Elon’s Edsel is no more. Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk revealed on social media that his car company is ending its failed attempt to wrest control of the American pickup truck market. The Cybertruck will cease production in the middle of 2027, liberating that space in Tesla’s cavernous factory for other uses—more Cybercabs, most likely. Musk first revealed the Cybertruck in late 2019, back when Tesla was still trading at a theoretically understandable price-to-earning ratio. The pickup's unusual angular shape owed more to low-res video game models than any concessions to practicality. At the time, Musk made fanciful claims that the truck would use a stainless steel monocoque construction, telling his audience that “the body and bed don’t do anything useful” on a normal truck. While some race cars use carbon-fiber monocoques for strength and lightness, making a pickup truck with a stainless steel monocoque chassis would only make sense if someone had an awful lot of stainless steel lying around and needed something to do with it all. The truck was supposed to go on sale for less than $40,000, and Tesla made its usual stratospheric sales predictions that (had they been accurate) the bare metal EVs would be as ubiquitous as the Model 3 and Y.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Voice AI infrastructure: The 2026 stack explained
articles.description: Explore every layer of voice AI infrastructure and AI agent architecture, from speech recognition to guardrails, with ElevenAgents examples.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Voice AI infrastructure is the set of models, connections, tools, and services that lets an AI agent listen to a call, decide what to do, take action in other systems, and answer out loud. And, with leading providers like ElevenLabs, all of this happens in a fraction of a second. A production voice agent runs on a stack of layers that includes speech recognition, turn-taking, a large language model, orchestration, tools, knowledge retrieval, speech synthesis, telephony, and monitoring. This guide explains the AI agent architecture behind a working voice agent. Each section converts what a layer does, why it matters in the wider infrastructure, and how ElevenAgents implements it, with Eleven v4 as the example voice layer. A voice agent turns audio into text, reasons based on that input, generates an answer, and then turns that response back into audio that the customer hears. That cascade of actions is made up by a robust stack of AI agent architecture. Here are the main layers that contribute to voice AI infrastructure in 2026: Together, these components work to create real-time conversations between AI agents and calling customers. The flow isn’t a straight line. ElevenAgents starts speaking after it receives “enough words and a comma” from the language model, meaning that audio begins playing before the full reply exists. Toll calls and retrieval run in the middle of a turn. Interruptions can arrive and are handled naturally by the agent while it generates speech. ElevenAgents supports two voice modes. In Custom mode, you pick the language model, the Text to Speech model, and the speech recognition settings yourself. In Realtime mode, you select an Eleven Realtime model and ElevenLabs manages those settings for you. Eleven Realtime v1 Mini is the default and has the lowest latency and cost. Eleven Realtime v1 Max reasons before it responds, which suits more complex instructions and cases where multi-step tool use is required. The system prompt, chosen voice, tools, attached knowledge base, and turn settings work the same in both modes. Custom mode is the better choice when you need a specific language model, a custom LLM, or a specific TTS model (for performance or latency optimization.) Speech recognition, also called ASR or speech to text, is the first layer of the stack. The model transcribes the caller's audio continuously while they speak. Doing so continuously allows the rest of the pipeline to start working before the sentence ends, saving on latency. Advanced models will handle everything from thick accents and different speaking speeds to background noise. Transcription is arguably one of the most important layers in the stack because any errors here will permeate through the rest of the stages. Mishear a booking reference? Wrong customer record actioned. Get a medication’s name wrong? Potential disaster. In its Trust Framework for Healthcare, ElevenLabs shows how high the stakes get with one misheard syllable: hydroxyzine versus hydralazine. ElevenAgents uses Scribe v2 Realtime, which transcribes speech in approximately 150 ms. ElevenLabs trained it for noisy backgrounds, diverse accents, and identifiers such as names, emails, and IDs. On the FLEURS multilingual benchmark across 30 languages, ElevenLabs reported the lowest word error rate of any low-latency ASR model. You enable it under the Advanced section of the agent configuration. In the same white paper mentioned above, ElevenLabs reports that Scribe v2 Medical leads every model on the public Eka Medical ASR benchmark at a 7.0% word error rate as of publication. Accurate (and rapid) transcription gives the next layers the clean input they need without adding significant latency. Turn taking is the set of rules that decides when the agent replies and when it listens. Being able to effectively understand turns in conversation and act upon them is what separates a conversation from a legacy IVR phone menu. There are a few functions that a turn taking component provides to voice AI infrastructure: A gap of about 200 ms is the typical gap between speakers in a human conversation. An agent that answers too early cuts callers off, while one that waits too long creates silences that make the call feel broken or unresponsive. For example, consider a caller who says "I'd like to book Friday afternoon, but..." and pauses. A silence timer replies at the pause and misses the qualification. A model that reads the words and the rhythm waits, allowing the user to finish, "It can’t be between 3 and 5 p.m., as I’ll be busy.” One agent misqualifies the caller’s intention and schedules the meeting at the wrong time. The other, with effective turn taking abilities, makes sure to avoid the specified time period. ElevenAgents runs a proprietary turn-taking model that analyzes tone, rhythm, and word context instead of relying on silence timers alone. When a caller interrupts, the signal that stops the agent lands in under 200 ms. ElevenLabs measures a median of ~150 ms from request to audible speech with Eleven v4 Turbo on ElevenAgents. The behavior is configurable via Conversation flow: Eager responds at the earliest opportunity. Normal is the balanced default. Patient waits longer and suits phone numbers, addresses, and emails. Starts the language model reply before the caller is confirmed finished. It cuts latency and can raise LLM cost. Turn them off when every word must be heard, such as legal disclaimers and safety instructions. Words such as "right" that should not interrupt the agent. Keeps the agent quiet when the caller says "give me a minute". Takes a turn after 1 to 30 seconds of silence. Use 5 to 10 seconds for casual conversations and 10 to 30 when callers need time to think. Plays filler speech such as "Hhmmmm...yeah." when the model is slow. Range 0.5 to 8 seconds, with 3 seconds recommended. An Enterprise setting that detects background voices and asks the caller to move somewhere quieter, at most once per conversation. Workflows can change turn eagerness mid-call. Your client also receives a vad_score event, a 0 to 1 probability that the user is speaking. Well-tuned turn-taking decides whether callers experience the agent as attentive or abrupt. For more on the concepts, see our full guide on turn taking. The large language model (LLM) is the reasoning layer. It reads the transcript, the instructions, and the conversation so far, then writes the response or decides to call a tool. A scripted voice bot recognizes a handful of commands. An LLM interprets requests phrased many different ways, holds context across turns, and decides when to retrieve information or hand off. Models differ in reasoning depth, speed, and cost. For a live voice conversation, response time matters as much as answer quality, so the model choice is a latency decision and a cost decision. ElevenAgents gives you one interface to models from Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic, plus open models hosted by ElevenLabs. You can also connect your own LLM by specifying an endpoint and storing credentials as secrets. ElevenLabs passes third-party LLM costs through at the provider's published rate with no markup. You can choose the model per subagent. The Enterprise Conversational Agent Playbook, Volume 2 recommends reserving higher-performance models for complex reasoning and using cheaper, low-latency models for tasks such as intent classification and FAQs. Providers have outages. LLM cascading handles them: if the primary model returns an API error, times out, or sends an empty response, ElevenAgents tries a backup sequence. The default timeout from primary to backup is 4 seconds, adjustable from 2 to 15 seconds, and the system makes at least 3 attempts across the available models. A custom LLM used as the primary model retries itself at least 3 times, unless you define your own backup order. The right model per task keeps the agent both fast and affordable. Agent orchestration coordinates the prompts, subagents, tools, and people involved in finishing a task. It decides what happens next at every point in the call. One agent with one long prompt grows hard to manage as responsibilities pile up. Orchestration splits the work into stages, each with its own instructions, model, and tools, and moves the caller between them. Smaller prompts are easier to test and cheaper to run, because each interaction loads less text. Splitting a flow lets a cheap model handle triage and FAQs and hands off to a stronger model only when a request needs it. Workflows in ElevenAgents are a visual builder for branching conversation graphs. Edges between nodes carry natural-language conditions that the LLM evaluates in real time. A support flow might start with a routing subagent on a fast model, send billing questions to a billing subagent on a stronger model, and finish with a transfer-to-number node when the caller asks for a person. After launch, the Workflow tab in analytics shows entries, average time spent, terminations, and edge distribution for each node. Orchestration turns a single agent into a system you can design, measure, and improve one node at a time. Function calling, also called tool calling, lets an agent request actions from external software that you have connected to your tech stack. It turns a question-answering interface into an agentic AI system that is able to complete work and interact with other tools on your behalf. Take a caller who asks to move tomorrow's appointment to Friday. The agent retrieves the booking, checks Friday's availability, updates the scheduling system, and confirms the change. Each step is a tool call that takes action. Tools are where conversations produce outcomes. Each tool needs clear inputs and outputs, and the agent needs to know whether a call succeeded before it tells the caller it did. ElevenAgents supports client tools that run in the user's application, webhook tools that call external APIs, code tools that run custom JavaScript in a sandbox on ElevenLabs infrastructure, MCP tools, and built-in system tools. The system tools include end call, language detection, agent transfer, transfer to number, skip turn, play keypad touch tone, and voicemail detection. You can add ambient audio while a tool runs and control whether callers can interrupt during execution. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for how applications give context and tools to language models. ElevenAgents connects to MCP servers over SSE and streamable HTTP. Workspace admins opt in first, since MCP is disabled by default for every workspace. You then choose an approval mode for each server: Always Ask, Fine-Grained Tool Approval, or No Approval. Client events such as client_tool_call and mcp_tool_call report tool activity, and the MCP event reports four states: loading, awaiting approval, success, and failure. Reliable tools give the agent real-world reach, and clear approval rules keep that reach under control. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives the agent facts from your own content, such as an internal fact database or wider client history log. Memory and personalization give it context about the caller that allows your agent to improve personalization and utility for your business. A language model has a training cutoff and no access to your documentation or records. RAG searches a knowledge base for each query, retrieves the most relevant passages, and supplies them to the model to give it the extra context needed for a useful response. Personalization data tells the agent who is calling and what is relevant to them. Grounding replies in approved content keeps answers accurate. Retrieval speed matters too, as every millisecond it adds is another that your customers will be waiting for. Personalization functions also stop callers from having to repeat information across different calls, as your agents will have the CRM records on hand at the start of each ne

articles.title: California man gets 14 years, 8 months for 150-mph fatal crash
articles.content: MARTINEZ, CA.— A northern California man has agreed to serve 14 years and eight months for killing a Castro Valley nurse while driving drunk at an estimated speed of 150 mph, court records show. Badal Devendra Dholaria, 28, of Pleasanton, was initially charged with murder in the Nov. 29, 2025, crash that killed 41-year-old Alix Sparks and injured her husband. But prosecutors agreed for Dholaria to plead no contest to manslaughter in exchange for the shorter prison term and dismissal of murder, court records show. Dholaria was sentenced on Oct. 15, but not until after he heard from Alix Sparks’ loved ones, including her husband, Gregory Sparks, who recounted surviving the crash and seeing his wife perish. “I watched the love of my life die in my arms in front of my eyes, all because a drunk driver with a new Tesla wanted to see how fast he could go,” Gregory Sparks said in court, the Pleasanton Weekly reported. The collision occurred near Crow Canyon and Bollinger Canyon roads in San Ramon. Dholaria later admitted to police that he had “two shots” before driving. Authorities estimated his speed at 150 mph, but say he’d slowed down to around 120 mph at the moment of impact. Someone witnessed him speeding and called police, but not within enough time for officers to find Dholaria and stop him before the collision. When they got there, police and firefighters told him to power down the Tesla, afraid that it was at higher risk of catching fire after the collision, but he was “argumentative” and refused, authorities said in court filings. Alix Sparks was declared dead at the crash site, and her husband was hospitalized with non-lifethreatening injuries, authorities said. Dholaria gets credit for the time he spent in jail while the case was pending. If he hadn’t accepted the plea deal, he was scheduled to go on trial Nov. 9, records show.

articles.title: Detroit violence interruption program has new evidence behind it. Now comes a push for permanence.
articles.description: This story was originally published by The Trace, a nonprofit newsroom covering gun violence in America. Sign up for its newsletters here. Detroit’s city-backed violence intervention program is showing significant promise in targeted areas as the city continues to experience record-level declines in gun violence, a University of Michigan evaluation has found. The ShotStopper community […]
articles.content: Homes the 48205 zip code area on Detroit’s east side on August 20th, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. Over decades, locals watched residents disappear, vacant homes multiply, and gun violence become a regular part of daily life in the 48205 zip code. Between 2017 and 2024, 732 people were shot in the zip code, including 151 who were killed giving the neighborhood the nickname “The Red Zone”. (Sylvia Jarrus for The Trace)This story was originally published by The Trace, a nonprofit newsroom covering gun violence in America. Sign up for its newsletters here. Detroit’s city-backed violence intervention program is showing significant promise in targeted areas as the city continues to experience record-level declines in gun violence, a University of Michigan evaluation has found. The ShotStopper community violence intervention (CVI) program operates in six zones across the city, where community groups create their own strategies to reduce gun violence. The program was launched in Detroit in 2023 and is unrelated to the ShotSpotter gun detection system. The evaluation found that areas with ShotStopper saw a 33 percent decrease in homicides in the three years since the program launched, versus 12 percent throughout the rest of the city. Nonfatal shootings declined by 38 percent in the six zones, compared to 28 percent outside of them. While researchers can’t definitively say the program directly caused the sharper declines, it’s a positive sign of the work done in the neighborhoods. “It looks like the teams did have significant influence on decreases in homicides and nonfatal shootings in their areas,” said Sam Stragand, a senior program manager at Poverty Solutions at the University of Michigan and co-author of the report. Detroit invested more than $11 million in ShotStopper over the last three years, giving community groups unusual autonomy to combat gun violence in their neighborhoods. With early evidence of success, the city now wants to make that experiment a permanent public safety strategy. What distinguishes ShotStoppers from other city-supported CVI programs across the country is the independence the organizations have in deciding how to prevent gun violence. The groups are rewarded for outperforming the citywide trends, meaning they can earn additional funding if shootings decline more sharply in their zones. “There’s a level of ‘Hey, you know your blocks and your neighborhoods better than anyone in the Mayor’s Office or any officer,’ so you do what you think is necessary,” said Mike Peterson, the director of ShotStoppers. “What fills in that work should be up to the groups, and their autonomy and their relationships and their capabilities.” For example, Force Detroit, a CVI group that works on the West Side, focuses more directly on those actively involved in shootings. New Era, which is located in the Northwest, takes a more community-wide approach and focuses more on engagement, local events, and providing resources for the community. The two groups have different approaches but they’re both part of ShotStoppers, and both have experienced success. “I think it’s safe to say that Force Detroit by far is the best performer out of the groups,” Stragand said. “New Era took a completely different approach and still had significant decreases in their area, as well.” The east side of Detroit has historically been one of the city’s hardest-hit areas for gun violence. Quincy Smith, who runs Team Pursuit, another ShotStoppers organization, said his team had to understand the history of the neighborhood to effectively interrupt cycles of violence. Smith points to a conflict between Bloods and Crips that escalated in the late 2000s, fueling an increase in shootings and heightened law enforcement presence. “I would say around 2010, you start to see the uptick in violence and then it gets to the point where if you’re caught on the wrong side of town, it was on sight,” Smith said, referring to a shoot-on-sight mentality among gang rivals. “From then, it was just ongoing.” That’s why Team Pursuit uses credible messengers with direct knowledge and experience in the longstanding conflicts to intervene at a street level before disputes turn violent. In the zone Team Pursuit now serves, nonfatal shootings dropped from 65 in the program’s first year to 19 in its second. “It’s remarkable the transition not only the community has gone through, but these guys have gone through,” Smith said, referring to the credible messengers working on the ground. Long-term funding for the program remains a question. ShotStoppers was initially funded by pandemic relief dollars. The city now supports it through its general fund, with some help from the state. For the 2025-2026 fiscal year, Detroit City Council approved an additional $3 million for ShotStopper. The city’s adopted 2026-2027 budget includes $10.8 million for community violence intervention, which is a $3.4 million increase from the previous year. Roughly $2.6 million in state public safety funding has also been earmarked to expand CVI efforts. While there’s no clear indication that the funding is in jeopardy, Peterson says it’s not yet considered a guaranteed part of the city’s budget. “We do want to get to a point where we can standardize this work and move it from a pilot program to a standing function within public safety in the city,” Peterson said. “ That’s something that comes with time.” Even if Detroit commits to ShotStoppers for the foreseeable future, the groups will still be working in neighborhoods struggling with disinvestment, limited economic opportunities, and social issues they cannot solve alone. “You can only hold the peace for so long when the underlying factors don’t change,” Stragand said. “As much as [the CVI groups] put into their work, there are also larger forces at play that also need to be addressed.”

articles.title: Detroit needs more special education teachers. MSU partnership aims to help.
articles.description: Detroit Public Schools Community District and Michigan State University launched an initiative where district teachers can pursue the university’s online master's degree in special education with an autism spectrum disorder (ASD) credential, or endorsement.
articles.content: The Detroit school district has launched a new partnership with Michigan State University to meet the growing demand of teachers certified in special education. Detroit Public Schools Community District and Michigan State University this fall launched an initiative where district teachers can pursue the university’s online master’s degree in special education with an autism spectrum disorder (ASD) credential, or endorsement. DPSCD covers the MSU program tuition, with 22 Detroit teachers enrolled in the fall cohort, said Erin Hamilton, MSU’s special education master’s program coordinator. “This intentional partnership allows us to have a pipeline in an area where it’s a growing need,” DPSCD Superintendent Nikolai Vitti told BridgeDetroit. “If we don’t do things like that, then our students won’t have certified teachers.” The initiative comes after Vitti earlier this year expressed concerns about special education certification, saying that the supply of educators statewide is not meeting demands when it comes to staffing and support for special education, particularly in ASD. There are 223,100 students receiving special education in the state, including students in private schools or homeschooling who receive special education services by a public school. About 13.5% of the students have ASD. DPSCD has also experienced a significant increase in the number of students diagnosed with ASD, going from 1,035 during the 2019–20 school year to 1,957 this school year, Vitti told BridgeDetroit, adding “which naturally means we need more teachers.” DPSCD, he said, has had a relationship with MSU in placing student teachers in the district through its Mentors as Teacher Educators, or MATE program. “But this (program) was very focused on identifying a problem and a need, which was the need to recruit and develop more teachers with the ASD endorsement certification,” he said. Students returned for their first day back to school at Bennett Elementary school on August 24, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. Credit: Sylvia Jarrus for Chalkbeat DPSCD began developing the MSU initiative earlier this year, after the district and the Detroit Federation of Teachers established an agreement in March to expand educators’ access to teacher preparation, tuition assistance, professional learning and pathways to state endorsements in high-need areas of special education, Vitti said. The district then began promoting the initiative internally, with interested teachers signing up through DPSCD’s human resources department. “Recruiting and developing special education teachers has been a growing challenge for us (DPSCD), throughout Michigan and throughout the country,” he said. Currently, an aspiring teacher needs a bachelor’s degree, completion of an approved teacher preparation program, complete clinical experiences, including student teaching, and pass the Michigan Test for Teacher Certification (MTTC). If they want to teach in special education, teachers must earn a specific categorical endorsement, such as ASD, cognitive impairment and speech and language impairment. Michigan has seen statewide teacher shortages as educators leave the field at an unsustainable rate. This has forced schools to rely on educators with temporary or interim credentials, according to a January report from the Education Policy Innovation Collaborative at MSU. That is especially true for special education, where vacancy rates are nearly double the statewide average, said the report. Across much of the state, the lack of staffing has resulted in teachers with no special education credentials instructing students with disabilities. The shortage is not only confined to teachers – Michigan also lacks speech language pathologists, social workers and paraprofessionals who work with students with disabilities. “This (partnership) comes at a perfect time,” Vitti said. “It’s a model for what the rest of Michigan should be doing, which is expanding partnerships and accelerated paid-for programs, so that teachers have an easier path to get this extra certification, or we’re not going to give our most vulnerable students what they deserve.” How does the program work? Vitti said participants must be full-time certified DPSCD teachers enrolled in a district-approved special education program. Educators are expected to complete the degree and certification requirements within three years of when they begin the program and must remain employed as a DPSCD teacher for six years from the time the program starts. Tuition for the participating cohort equates to $200,000, which is being paid for under the district’s general fund, Vitti said. Hamilton said special education is one of the hardest areas to staff and MSU’s partnership with DPSCD is a way the two institutions can grow a pipeline from within the system. “Tuition support removes the cost barrier that keeps many good teachers from pursuing an endorsement,” she said. “The commitment to stay as a DPSCD classroom teacher for six years helps the district keep that expertise in Detroit schools. For Detroit, that means more teachers prepared to support students with autism. For Michigan, it’s a model other districts and universities could look at.” The online master’s degree in special education requires 30 to 36 credits, depending on an educator’s previous preparation and teaching certification, Vitti said. Hamilton said program participants will have to complete six courses focused on evidence-based practices for supporting students with autism, including communication and social supports, inclusive instructional approaches and strategies for addressing individual learning needs. “They will learn to assess academic and behavioral needs, design instructional and behavioral interventions, work with families and school teams, and create structured, predictable classrooms,” she said. “Teachers who finish the sequence and pass the ASD Michigan Test for Teacher Certification (MTTC) can meet the state requirements for the ASD endorsement.” Tuition for the participating cohort equates to $200,000, which is being paid for under the district’s general fund, Vitti said. Credit: Jamie Kelter Davis for Chalkbeat Teachers will then be able to teach in DPSCD’s ASD program. The district offers special education hubs across its schools, which are designed for students to get the services they need, while still being mainstreamed in general education schools. Vitti said he’s open to expanding the program so teachers can take courses at other colleges in Michigan. “If colleges and universities are going to be better partners, then these are the exact kind of programs that they need to offer to be relevant and helpful,” he said. Heather Eckner, director of statewide education for the Autism Alliance of Michigan, said the initiative is a “positive” as the state looks to create more avenues for special education-endorsed educators. “This sounds great, and I wonder how scalable it is for other areas of the state,” she said. “Does MSU have the capacity to partner with multiple districts, or are they trying to pilot something with Detroit right now?” Hamilton said she couldn’t speak to future partnership plans for MSU. ‘A step in the right direction’ The new initiative comes at a time where the Michigan Department of Education is looking at ways to make it easier for educators to become certified in special education. Last month, the agency proposed making changes to its Michigan Administrative Rules for Special Education (MARSE). One of those changes includes a new stand-alone special education teacher endorsement. Teachers must be prepared to provide specially designed instruction in reading and math development, core content in general education, and positive student educational outcomes, according to MDE. With the stand-alone endorsement, teachers can be placed in special education programs such as: Mild cognitive impairment Emotional impairment Specific learning disabilities Physical or other health impaired Elementary and secondary resource However, the endorsement cannot be used for programs like ASD, visual impairment and severe and moderate cognitive impairment, MDE stated. Those disabilities would still require a separate endorsement. The timeline of the proposed changes can take up to 90 days depending upon several factors, including review of all public comments, submission to the Joint Committee on Administrative Rules (JCAR) and subsequent adoption, MDE spokesperson Bob Wheaton told Bridge Michigan. Vitti said the proposed rule change is a start, but he doesn’t believe that all teachers will pursue an ASD endorsement. He believes the state should allow teachers certified in special education to teach in multiple areas and then commit to getting their endorsement certification within a certain number of years. “We still need more flexibility because the reality of the market is we don’t have enough (teachers),” he said. “MDE and universities and districts can do a lot better with incentivizing teachers to go in these fields because if we don’t start incentivizing…we’re not going to have certified teachers, and that’s not a conversation just for Detroit, but across the state.”

90-year-old Holocaust survivor dies almost a year after being shot in the Sydney Hanukkah massacre
articles.description: 90-year-old Holocaust survivor dies almost a year after being shot in the Sydney Hanukkah massacre AP News Australian woman shot during Bondi Beach attack dies almost a year later BBC Bondi beach shooting: Eva Geller, 90, shot during massacre dies in hospital year after antisemitic attack The Guardian Holocaust survivor, 90, injured in Bondi massacre dies nearly a year after attack The Times of Israel 90yo woman shot
articles.content: MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — A 90-year-old Holocaust survivor has died almost a year after she was wounded during the massacre of 15 people at a Sydney Hanukkah celebration, officials said Friday. Romanian-born Eva Geller died Thursday night in a Sydney hospital, Executive Council of Australian Jewry director Evan Zlatkis said. She was one of around 40 people wounded when two gunmen allegedly inspired by the Islamic State group opened fire on a crowd at Bondi Beach on Dec. 14. Fifteen victims aged 10 to 87 died. One of the gunmen, Sajid Akram, was shot dead by police at the scene. Rabbi Aron Moss said Geller had been “strong and pretty healthy right up until the Bondi attack where she was shot.” She had been admitted to the hospital several times in recent weeks due to surgery complications, Moss said. “She’s a proud mother, grandmother and great grandmother. A beautiful, positive person who even in these difficult months maintained her positivity,” Moss said on the family’s behalf. “She was told after being shot that she will never walk again by the doctors. But through sheer determination, she got back up and she did walk again,” Moss added. She walked with a cane following the leg wound, he said. The surviving alleged gunman, Naveed Akram, the 25-year-old son of the dead gunman, has been charged with 15 counts of murder, 43 of attempted murder and one of committing a terrorist act. He has yet to enter a plea. It was not yet clear whether Geller’s death would change the charges Akram faces. Police said in a statement they were awaiting advice from a state coroner, who would investigate the circumstances of her death. Akram is scheduled to appear in court next on Feb. 24, when prosecutors expect to finalize what charges will go to the New South Wales state Supreme Court for trial. State Premier Chris Minns offered his condolences to Geller’s family. “After everything Geller endured, the news of her death is heartbreaking,” Minns said in a statement. “Almost a year on, we are still living with the pain and aftershock of that evil act. We will never forget Eva or any victim whose life was changed forever,” Minns added. (Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)In an executive order issued Thursday, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer directed executive departments and agencies to conduct a review of “all policies, procedures, and practices governing the collection, maintenance, storage, and retention of records and data relating to an individual’s reproductive health” and revise any such policies in order to ensure the privacy of that data. The review must include, but is not limited to, any precise geolocation information derived from an individual’s internet-connected device and any existing data-sharing agreements or contracts. “This executive directive is another important step in keeping our patients and providers safe,” Whitmer said in a press release. “Data misuse is a growing threat, and we must make sure that reproductive care data never lands in the hands of people who could weaponize it. I’m proud to sign this executive directive to secure Michiganders’ reproductive health data and strengthen patients’ confidence as they seek reproductive care.” According to a news release from Whitmer’s office, reproductive care includes, but is not limited to, prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, contraception, sterilization, abortion care, miscarriage management, and infertility care. Whitmer supports legislation that would protect reproductive health data The directive, which bars sharing geolocation information and other data with commercial organizations and federal agencies, takes effect immediately and requires departments with relevant records to submit a report to the governor’s office detailing their findings and any policy changes. Reproductive rights advocates celebrated Whitmer’s order as she enters the final months of her term, with Planned Parenthood of Michigan President and CEO Paula Thornton Greear thanking Whitmer for her work in office. “Nobody should have to fear that accessing sexual and reproductive health care could endanger them,” Thornton Greear said. “That protection reaches someone getting prenatal care, a family going through infertility treatment, a patient managing a miscarriage, a student picking up birth control, and anyone who needs an abortion. Every one of them deserves to know that seeking care in Michigan won’t leave a trail someone can use against them.” That was a change in tone from earlier this year when Planned Parenthood of Michigan asked Whitmer to provide $5 million to prevent the closure of health centers around the state amid attacks and funding cuts from the Trump administration. When the governor said the agency would need to look to the Legislature for assistance, Greear said Michigan patients were “not a football to be tossed around from branch to branch of the government,” and that Whitmer needed “to take responsibility and … drive a solution forward.” Less than two months later, Planned Parenthood of Michigan announced it was permanently closing clinics in Lansing, Livonia and Warren.

articles.title: Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy AI agent security startup Clutch for $500M
articles.description: Clutch, backed by Lightspeed and SignalFire, was last valued at $85 million, according to a source.
articles.content: Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security, a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions. Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source. The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies. Palo Alto Networks and Clutch Security did not respond to a request for comment. The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions. The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily. Upwind, a startup using AI to secure cloud infrastructure, recently turned down an acquisition offer from Datadog that valued it at roughly 40 times ARR, TechCrunch reported last week. If the deal happens, it would be Palo Alto Networks’ seventh acquisition this year, according to PitchBook. The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks. In September, Palo Alto Networks acquired Console, a two-year-old startup that uses AI agents to automate routine IT help desk tasks. The transaction valued Console at $500 million in stock and cash, TechCrunch reported. Other VC-backed companies that Palo Alto Networks has scooped up this year include NEA-backed Embrace, for $325 million; Chronosphere, an observability platform backed by Greylock and Lux Capital, for $2.95 billion; and Koi, a cyber startup backed by Battery and Team8, for $231 million, according to regulatory filings. Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired. Cyera, a cybersecurity startup valued at $12 billion earlier this year, acquired Oasis Security, which, like Clutch, focuses on managing AI agents’ access to systems, for $1 billion. Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million, Calcalist reported. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission.
